# Research Participation (for Undergrad Students)
MLLab always welcomes undergraduate students to participate in research. The projects below are the research topics that the lab is currently interested in and intends to proceed. Interested undergraduate students should check the list before applying for research participation and contact their advisor via email. This page will be continuously updated. (Last modified 2026-10-14)
# Machine Learning Free Topics - Advisors: All
Any other interesting research ideas other than the topics listed below? It looks interesting, but are you wondering if this is also machine learning research? If you want to learn machine learning but don't know where to start, feel free to contact us anytime!
# Learning to Combat the Hallucination of Large Language Models - Advisor: Sangdon Park
Large Language Models (LLMs) confidently generate wrong information, which undermines the trust of LLMs as a knowledge base. How to mitigate this?
This question has been actively emerged due to the power of ChatGPT.
In this research project, we will explore learning methods (e.g., conformal prediction) to answer this question.
References
Andrew Ng’s Twitter Post on the overconfidence of LLMs
Sangdon Park and Taesoo Kim PAC Neural Prediction Set Learning to Quantify the Uncertainty of Generative Language Models arXiv 2023
# Experience-Driven Self-Evolving Robotic Planning - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Seungjoon Lee
Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled robots to autonomously generate and refine action plans and control programs. However, existing approaches often suffer from unreliable knowledge accumulated through experience, costly trial-and-error, and excessive LLM inference overhead. We aim to develop robotic planning agents that continuously improve from their own experiences while minimizing computational costs. Our research focuses on (1) learning from successes and failures while correcting erroneous knowledge, (2) improving token efficiency in failure analysis and plan code generation, and (3) minimizing runtime latency to enable fast and responsive execution when deployed on real-world robots. Through these efforts, we seek to build robust and efficient robotic agents that autonomously evolve their planning capabilities across diverse tasks and environments.
References
Lu, Runyu, et al. "ASPIRE: Agentic Skills Discovery for Robotics" arXiv 2026.
Lee, Seungjoon, et al. "Experience-based Knowledge Correction for Robust Planning in Minecraft" ICLR 2026.
# LLMs for Code Vulnerability Discovery - Advisor: Sangdon Park
Finding source or binary code vulnerabilities is a long-standing and never-ending problem. The recent advance in LLMs potentially provides clues to further advance the current code vulnerability discovery performance. In this project, we will explore the potentials of LLMs in finding code vulnerabilities.
# Deep Learning Application for Scientific Discovery - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Seungbeom Lee
This research focuses on applying deep learning to the field of scientific discovery. Specifically, we aim to build model architectures tailored to each scientific domain while efficiently incorporating inductive biases, such as geometric priors, to address various scientific challenges.
Our work has broad applications in areas such as molecule generation, molecular property prediction and drug-target binding pose estimation.
References
Ying, Chengxuan, et al. "Do Transformers Really Perform Bad for Graph Representation?" NeurIPS 2021.
Corso, Gabriele, et al. "DiffDock: Diffusion Steps, Twists, and Turns for Molecular Docking" ICLR 2023.
Xu, Minkai, et al. "Geodiff: A geometric diffusion model for molecular conformation generation." ICLR 2022.
# Theoretical Analysis for Online Learning - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Seockbean Song
Online learning involves algorithms that make decisions and learn from data sequentially. We aim to develop a solid theoretical foundation to understand and evaluate the performance of these methods. In this project, students will study the core principles of online learning, including performance analysis, regret minimization, and the development of provably efficient algorithms.
References
Song, Seockbean, et al. "Rising Multi-Armed Bandits with Known Horizons" arXiv 2026.
Song, Seockbean, et al. "Combinatorial Rising Bandits" ICLR 2026.
# Machine Unlearning in Text-to-Image Generative Models - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Saemi Moon, Minjong Lee
Generative models have made significant advancements in producing high-quality images, but they also pose risks by potentially generating harmful, explicit, or privacy- and copyright-infringing content. To address these concerns, we aim to develop methods that allow models to “unlearn” problematic concepts, thereby enhancing the ethical and safe deployment of these models.
References
Moon, Saemi, Seunghyuk Cho, and Dongwoo Kim. "Feature Unlearning for Pre-trained GANs and VAEs" AAAI 2024.
Kumari, Nupur, et al. "Ablating Concepts in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models" NeurIPS 2023.
Gandikota, Rohit, et al. "Erasing Concepts from Diffusion Models" ICCV 2023.
# Reward Models for Personalized LLMs - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Youngbin Choi
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) allows models to generate outputs aligned with human preferences, such as helpfulness and harmfulness. However, current reward models tend to reflect majority preferences, often neglecting those of individuals or minority groups. This study aims to create personalized reward models to enable the development of more individualized language models (LLMs).
References
Chakraborty, Qiu, et al., "MaxMin-RLHF: Towards Equitable Alignment of Large Language Models with Diverse Human Preferences" ICML 2024.
Siththaranjan, Laidlaw, et al. "Distributional Preference Learning: Understanding and Accounting for Hidden Context in RLHF" ICLR 2024.
Poddar, Wan, et al. "Personalizing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with Variational Preference Learning" arXiv 2024.
# Uncertainty Learning via Conformal Prediction - Advisor: Sangdon Park
As ML models are used in practical environments, e.g., ChatGPT or drones, the concerns on the trustworthiness of model predictions have been greatly emerged. In particular, we are interested in rigorous uncertainty learning as the basis for the correctness of predictions, and conformal prediction is a promising method for rigorous uncertainty learning. However, its correctness guarantees depend on the assumptions of data distributions. In this research project, we explore and design practical learning algorithms for conformal prediction under various distributional assumptions.
References
Vladimir Vovk et al. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World 2005
Anastasios Angelopoulos et al. Uncertainty Sets for Image Classifiers using Conformal Prediction ICLR 2021
Sangdon Park et al. PAC Confidence Sets for Deep Neural Networks via Calibrated Prediction ICLR 2020
# Controllable Visual Content Generation and Editing - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Sunung Mun
Recent advances in generative AI have enabled realistic image and video synthesis and editing, yet precise control remains challenging. Existing models often introduce unintended changes during editing, struggle with complex instructions, or fail to preserve fine-grained details of reference objects. We aim to develop more controllable and reliable generative models, focusing on (1) precise and localized visual editing, (2) compositional content generation, and (3) reference-based generation with fine-grained detail and identity preservation. We explore diffusion models, vision-language models, and inference-time verification and refinement to improve generation fidelity and controllability.
References
Mun, Sunung, et al. "EPIC: Efficient Predicate-Guided Inference-Time Control for Compositional Text-to-Image Generation" NeurIPS 2026.
Mun, Sunung, et al. "Addressing Text Embedding Leakage in Diffusion-based Image Editing" ICCV 2025.
# Efficiency in Software Engineering Agents - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Seunghyuk Cho
Large language model (LLM) agents, e.g., Claude code and Codex, now resolve real-world software engineering (SWE) issues, but at a high cost: multi-agent SWE systems repeatedly re-explore the same repository, spending a large amount of tokens, latency, and energy on redundant search.
In this work, we study how to make SWE agents efficient without sacrificing their issue-solving ability, e.g., by sharing retrieved context across agents and turns, designing persistent sub-agents, and rethinking the agent-computer interface.
References
Seunghyuk Cho, et al., "Long Live the Librarian! A Persistent Search Sub-Agent for Energy-Efficient Multi-Agent Software Engineering Systems" EMNLP 2026.
Carlos E. Jimenez, et al., "SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?" ICLR 2024.
# Reasoning and Discovery with LLMs - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Sungjae Lee
We study how large language models (LLMs) reason through challenging problems and discover new insights and solutions. Our interests range from mathematical reasoning and program synthesis to agentic tasks involving tools and external environments. We investigate how individual models explore and refine ideas, as well as new ways for multiple agents to interact. This includes studying how agents exchange partial insights, challenge assumptions, and build on one another's reasoning. Participants will develop and analyze reasoning methods, exploring how these processes can support the discovery of new knowledge and solutions while improving reliability and efficiency.
References
Lee, Sungjae, et al. "Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation" Preprint.
Lee, Sungjae, et al. "Semantic Exploration with Adaptive Gating for Efficient Problem Solving with Language Models" ACL 2025.
# Model IP Protection - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Minwoo Jang
AI models are valuable assets built with substantial GPU resources, large-scale datasets, and considerable time and effort. Techniques such as model merging, distillation, and fine-tuning have enabled efficient model adaptation and reuse, but they can also be exploited to modify or reproduce models without authorization from the original developers. Our research focuses on protecting model intellectual property (IP) by preventing and/or detecting unauthorized model reuse. Through these efforts, we aim to establish the technical foundations for model provenance and sovereignty.
References
Jang, Minwoo, et al. "Retrospective Distillation Attribution via Normalized Response Similarity" arXiv 2026.
Sakamoto, Keitaro, et al. "Locking Pretrained Weights via Deep Low-Rank Residual Distillation" NeurIPS 2026.
Jang, Minwoo, et al. "Making Models Unmergeable via Scaling-Sensitive Loss Landscape" ICML 2026.
Savani, Yash, et al. "Antidistillation Sampling" NeurIPS 2025.
# Security and Privacy of LLMs - Advisor: Sangdon Park
The power of LLMs and their daily life use bring concerns on security and privacy issues (e.g., vulnerable code generation and privacy leakage). Then, how severe are the security and privacy issues? How to efficiently and effectively unlearn the issues in LLMs? In this project, we will evaluate LLMs security and privacy concerns and design learning algorithms for mitigation.
# From Uncertainty to Better Decision - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Minhyeon Oh
Making informed decisions under uncertainty is a fundamental challenge for AI systems operating in real-world environments. Critical information is often missing or cannot be directly observed, requiring AI systems to actively determine what they need to know before making decisions. This research explores how AI systems can identify decision-relevant information, acquire it efficiently through interaction, and use the resulting evidence to make more reliable decisions.
References
Oh, Minhyeon, et al. "Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents" Preprint.
Oh, Minhyeon, et al. "Comparison-based Active Preference Learning for Multi-dimensional Personalization" ACL 2025.
# LLMs in Interactive Environments - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Minjong Lee
LLMs solve problems by interacting with diverse entities: having multi-turn conversations with humans, collaborating with other LLM agents, and interacting with environments such as web pages and code repositories. Our research aims to improve LLMs so that they can interact more effectively across these interactive settings.
References
Choi, Youngbin, et al. In-Place Feedback: Reliable Refinement for Multi-Turn Expert-LLM Collaboration arXiv 2025
Shinn, Noah, et al. Reflexion: Language agents with verbal reinforcement learning NeurIPS 2023
Liang, Tian, et al. Encouraging divergent thinking in large language models through multi-agent debate EMNLP 2024
# Towards Efficient Distributed LLMs: Mixture-of-Experts, Multi-Agent Systems and Federated Learning - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Jabin Koo
As large language models (LLMs) grow to hundreds of billions of parameters, they must be trained and served across many GPUs, making the efficiency of the underlying distributed system as important as the model itself. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale models by activating only a few experts per token, while multi-agent systems divide complex tasks among specialized agents running on a shared backbone. For example, in multi-agent workflows, each agent's role determines which experts it actually needs, so far fewer experts can be kept in memory, while in large-scale training and serving, how experts and tokens are distributed across devices decides how much time is lost to communication. This approach is particularly important at scale, where memory, inter-GPU communication, and load imbalance, rather than raw computation, become the main bottlenecks. In this study, we explore how to co-design model architectures, algorithms, and distributed systems to make LLMs faster, cheaper, and more scalable.
References
Koo, Jabin, et al. "Dynamic Expert Pruning for Multi-Agent Systems" arXiv 2026.
Koo, Jabin, et al. "Federated Variational Preference Alignment with Gumbel-Softmax Prior for Personalized User Preferences" ICML 2026.
Koo, Jabin, et al. "Towards Robust and Efficient Federated Low-Rank Adaptation with Heterogeneous Clients" ACL 2025.
# Graph Learning Enhancement by Structural Modifications - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Jaeseung Heo
Using high-quality data is crucial for training accurate machine learning models. Graph data, which includes structural information in the form of edges, offers unique opportunities for improving model performance. Graph learning enhancement aims to refine this structural information by removing noise and emphasizing more informative patterns. Techniques such as edge rewiring, which modifies connections between nodes, node dropping, which removes less important nodes, and label smoothing, which adjusts labels to reduce overconfidence, all leverage the inherent relationships in the graph to improve model accuracy and generalization.
References
Yu Rong, et al., "DropEdge: Towards Deep Graph Convolutional Networks on Node Classification" ICLR 2020.
Xiaotian Han, et al., "G-Mixup: Graph Data Augmentation for Graph Classification" ICML 2022.
Kaixiong Zhou, et al. "Adaptive Label Smoothing To Regularize Large-Scale Graph Training" SDM 2023.

# Model IP Protection - Advisor: Jungseul Ok, Mentor: Minwoo Jang
AI models are valuable assets built with substantial GPU resources, large-scale datasets, and considerable time and effort. Techniques such as model merging, distillation, and fine-tuning have enabled efficient model adaptation and reuse, but they can also be exploited to modify or reproduce models without authorization from the original developers. Our research focuses on protecting model intellectual property (IP) by preventing and/or detecting unauthorized model reuse. Through these efforts, we aim to establish the technical foundations for model provenance and sovereignty.

References
Jang, Minwoo, et al. "Retrospective Distillation Attribution via Normalized Response Similarity" arXiv 2026.
Sakamoto, Keitaro, et al. "Locking Pretrained Weights via Deep Low-Rank Residual Distillation" NeurIPS 2026.
Jang, Minwoo, et al. "Making Models Unmergeable via Scaling-Sensitive Loss Landscape" ICML 2026.
Savani, Yash, et al. "Antidistillation Sampling" NeurIPS 2025.

# Machine Unlearning in Text-to-Image Generative Models - Advisor: Dongwoo Kim, Mentor: Saemi Moon, Minjong Lee
Generative models have made significant advancements in producing high-quality images, but they also pose risks by potentially generating harmful, explicit, or privacy- and copyright-infringing content. To address these concerns, we aim to develop methods that allow models to “unlearn” problematic concepts, thereby enhancing the ethical and safe deployment of these models.

References

# Security and Privacy of LLMs - Advisor: Sangdon Park
The power of LLMs and their daily life use bring concerns on security and privacy issues (e.g., vulnerable code generation and privacy leakage). Then, how severe are the security and privacy issues? How to efficiently and effectively unlearn the issues in LLMs? In this project, we will evaluate LLMs security and privacy concerns and design learning algorithms for mitigation.

raw.name: 조직 재생 및 발달 연구실 (Laboratory of Tissue Regeneration & Development)

intro.text:
Laboratory of Tissue Regeneration & Development
조직 재생 및 발달 연구실
Tissue Regeneration & Development
조직 재생 및 발달 연구실에서는 마우스 피부와 배아를 모델로 하여 창상 이후 조직의 치유 및 재생, 그리고 배아 발생 중 조직 발달의 역학에 대해 연구합니다.
POSTECH Bio Open Innovation Center(BOIC) room 3006
Tel : 054-279-2295
hur9111@postech.ac.kr

In the Laboratory of Tissue Regeneration and Development, we are dedicated to unraveling the intricate dynamics of tissue repair and development, employing mouse skin and embryos as our model systems. Our research initiatives delve into the complexities of wound healing process and the sophisticated landscape of tissue development, including embryonic growth.
At the core of our investigations lies a comprehensive exploration of the roles played by stem cells, emphasizing their intercellular communication within the tissue microenvironment, occurring in diverse forms, including extracellular vesicles. Navigating the elaborate system of cellular communication, differentiation, and regeneration, our objective is to elucidate the underlying mechanisms governing these processes. Ultimately, our goal is to provide innovative therapeutic strategies that advance regenerative medicine and effectively address tissue-related disorders.
•Tissue repair and regeneration
- Stem cell biology
- Intercellular communication & Extracellular vesicles
- Aging
•Tissue development
- Embryonic development
- Cellular senescence
Research topics
•Investigating the interaction between tissue-resident stem cells and their microenvironment during the process of skin wound healing.
•Exploring the roles played by intercellular communication via extracellular vesicles (i.e. microvesicles and exosomes) in the wound healing process.
•Studying the effects of aging-induced changes in stem cells on delayed wound healing.
•Unraveling the mechanisms and significance of intercellular communication during mammalian embryonic development.
•Understanding the contributions of cellular senescence to wound healing and embryonic development.
조직 재생 및 발달 연구실에서는 크게 다음과 같은 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
•조직 재생 연구
조직이 손상되었을 때 조직의 치유와 재생에 대해 연구합니다. 조직 내의 성체 줄기세포가 어떠한 역할을 하는지에 집중하며, 특히 줄기세포와 주변 미세환경과의 상호작용이 조직 전반의 재생에 미치는 영향에 대해 알아봅니다. 마우스 피부 창상 모델을 이용하여 조직 재생 과정의 기전을 밝히고, 재생 의학적인 관점에서 창상 지연에 대한 새로운 접근법을 찾는 것을 목표로 합니다.
•조직 발달 연구
배아 발생 동안 조직 발달의 역학에 대해 연구합니다. 조직 발달 과정에서 줄기세포의 역할을 규명하고, 조직 발달에 영향을 미치는 다양한 인자들의 상호작용을 연구합니다. 마우스 배아를 모델로 하여 배아 내 세포 간 상호작용이 조직과 기관의 발달에 미치는 영향과 그 기전을 알아보고, 장기적으로는 발달 중 발생할 수 있는 질병의 치료 전략을 제시하고자 합니다.
주요 연구 주제는 다음과 같습니다.
•피부 창상 치유 과정에서 줄기세포와 주변 미세환경 사이의 상호작용 연구
•노화에 따른 성체 줄기세포의 변화와 이에 따른 창상 치유 지연 기전 연구
•포유류 배아 발생 중 세포 간 상호작용 기전과 그 역할 연구
•창상 치유 과정 동안 세포외소포체 (extracellular vesicle; microvesicle & exosome)를 통한 세포 간 정보 전달의 역할 연구
•창상 치유와 배아 발생 과정 동안 세포 노화 (cellular senescence)의 발생 기전과 역할 연구
학부생은 본 실험실 연구 참여를 통해 위의 주제에 대해 연구하는 동안 생명과학 연구에 필요한 다양한 실험 기법을 배울 수 있습니다.
세포분자생물학 기법
- 조직/세포 형광 면역 염색 후 현미경 관찰 및 이미지 분석
- 세포배양
- Western blot, conventional PCR, qRT-PCR
- 바이러스 벡터와 리포솜을 이용한 세포 형질전환
마우스 실험 기법
- 마우스 핸들링 및 브리딩
- 조직 미세해부 (microdisection)
- 마우스 배아 해부 및 배아 전체 염색 (whole mount staining)
기타 실험 기법
- 유세포 분리 (FACS; Fluorescence-activated cell sorting)와 분석 (FACS analysis)
- H&E 염색 및 조직학적 분석
- 유전자 발현 조절을 알아보기 위한 시퀀싱 결과 분석

intro.text:
Photonic Cluster States
Stationary Light Polaritons
Quantum Communication
Quantum and Classical Interferometric Metrology
Quantum computing operates using quantum bits (qubits) that exploit uniquely quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to solve problems that are challenging for classical computers. One-way quantum computer, also known as measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) performs complex algorithms by making a sequence of measurements on a highly entangled state called a cluster state. Large cluster states can be realized by fusing smaller cluster states, which can be done using linear optics with photonic qubits. Our lab focuses on generating multi-qubit cluster states using photonic qubits generated via spontaneous parametric down conversion (SPDC). We are also working toward demonstrating complex quantum algorithms and quantum simulations based on large cluster states and feedforward measurements.

Photonic Cluster States
Quantum computing operates using quantum bits (qubits) that exploit uniquely quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to solve problems that are challenging for classical computers. One-way quantum computer, also known as measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) performs complex algorithms by making a sequence of measurements on a highly entangled state called a cluster state. Large cluster states can be realized by fusing smaller cluster states, which can be done using linear optics with photonic qubits. Our lab focuses on generating multi-qubit cluster states using photonic qubits generated via spontaneous parametric down conversion (SPDC). We are also working toward demonstrating complex quantum algorithms and quantum simulations based on large cluster states and feedforward measurements.

Stationary Light Polaritons
Stationary light pulse (SLP) represents a striking manifestation of coherent light-matter interaction, where a light pulse is effectively brought to a standstill within an atomic medium. This phenomenon arises through the interplay of counter-propagating control fields in systems exhibiting electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). At POSTECH, we explore experimental techniques to generate and control SLP using cold atomic ensembles and tailored laser fields. Our research aims to implement stationary pulse as a platform for quantum memory, nonlinear optics at the single-photon level, and quantum information processing. Ultimately, SLP offers a promising route toward controlled light-matter quantum interfaces.

Quantum Communication
Quantum cryptography utilizes the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics to achieve secure communication. At POSTECH, we conduct research on developing and implementing entanglement-based quantum communication, where security is guaranteed by the nonlocal correlations of entangled photon pairs. We explore efficient methods for generating and distributing entangled photons using spontaneous parametric down-conversion. In particular, we investigate hyperentanglement, where multiple degrees of freedom, such as polarization and time-bin, are entangled simultaneously, to enhance the performance and scalability of quantum communication systems. Such multi-dimensional entanglement offers advantages in noise resilience and information capacity, paving the way for the next generation of quantum communication networks.

Quantum and Classical Interferometric Metrology
Quantum metrology and sensing can achieve high sensitivity and resolution beyond the standard quantum limit. While entangled states of N photons are traditionally associated with reaching the so-called Heisenberg limit—where measurement uncertainty scales as 1/N—this is not the only pathway to such precision. Our lab has demonstrated Heisenberg-limited scaling using iterative interactions, a practical approach that enhances measurement sensitivity without requiring entanglement. Another central concept in quantum metrology is the Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB), which is the theoretical lower bound on estimation uncertainty for a given quantum state and measurement scheme. We have developed and experimentally implemented adaptive estimation techniques that saturate the QCRB, thereby achieving optimal precision. Our work spans both theoretical and experimental aspects of high-precision parameter estimation using quantum resources and techniques, including weak value amplification, iterative measurement strategies, and other advanced quantum measurement protocols.

intro.text:
Inorganic Synthesis
Solution Growth
A high degree of control over the size, structure, and composition of nanocrystals is essential to tune their chemical and physical properties for target applications. In particular, 2D nanocrystals of different sizes have been investigated extensively owing to their superior electrical, optical, and thermal properties. In reaction system, precursor, surfactant, reductant determines the final shape of synthesized materials due to different surface energies of different crystallographic planes.
We aim to control the structure of synthesized materials by controlling reaction environment.
On-substrate Synthesis
Thin films of crystalline layer‐structured 2D materials have been studied for decades, as they exhibit a wide range of unique electrical, optical, thermal, and mechanical properties, which are not observed in their bulk counterparts. Those 2D thin films hold a great promise for a variety of applications in the field of future electronics, optics, energy storage, and catalysis.
To obtain thin films of nanomaterials on desired substrates, elemental source(precursor) is first drop-casted or spin-coated on Si/ITO/FTO substrate. Next, substrate is heated using microwave oven or rapid thermal annealing(RTA) system to increase the temperature of substrate. Heating induces precursor decomposition, chemical reaction, crystal development selectively on substrate, enabling thin film synthesis possible. Our interest is focused on transition metal dichalcogenides(TMDC; MoS2, WS2, MoSe2 ⋯) and metal oxides(HfO2, Al2O3 ⋯).

Stretchable Electronics
Material design for Stretchable Electronics
Stretchable Conductor
Stretchable electronics are having great interests because of their wide availability in wearable devices, soft robotics, and implants. For the stretchable electronics, one of the most important and fundamental components is stretchable conductor. Stretchable conductor must maintain their original mechanical, and electrical performance despite of the stretching cycles. Our lab research aims the development of structural, and intrinsically stretchable conducting materials as a basic component for stretchable electronics for the actual use of display, transistor, sensors, and batteries. Mechanical monitoring of our body is an emerging requirement for next generation human-friendly electronics, which can measure not only tiny bio-signals such as wrist pulse, apexcardiogram and facial expression, but large motions like joint and muscle motions. Strain sensing is a basic function of the sensor system and the physical intimacy could be acquired with softness or stretchability of the materials comprising sensors. Tactile sensing is the most important function comprising electronic skin system. As a substitute for mechanoreceptor in human skin, it feels external mechanical stimulation like pressure and strain and transduces to electrical signals. Film type high sensitive pressure sensor has been used to measure small bio-signals. In our lab, we are fabricating various type of pressure sensor matrix array for different purpose. On-skin sensors measured pressure profiles in small scale like human cutaneous system, that were utilized as Braille scanner and also showed potentials for prosthetics or robot skin application. Additionally, we are also interested in active tactile sensors using self-power generating system.

Bioelectrical Signal Sensor
Recently, people want to take care their health condition in real time. There are electrical signals from our body such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalogram…etc. These signals help us to diagnose health condition of our body. Mobile healthcare devices want to measure these electrical signals. To measure these signals, it is important to have conformal contact between the sensor and the skin. Because skin shows dynamic movement, this sensor should be stretchable. The device also should have breathability and make sweat evaporate easily for long-term use. All materials in the sensor must be biocompatible and robust. In our lab, bioelectrical signal sensors are fabricated using hydrogels, conductive polymers and nanoparticles. In the future, we will develop this research from on-skin wearable sensors to implantable sensors.

raw.name: 인공 복합 산화물 연구실 (Artificial Complex Oxide Lab (ACOL))

intro.text:
Research

Pioneering the Future of Complex Oxide Epitaxial Thin Films
At ACOL, our journey begins at the frontier of condensed matter physics & materials science. We dive deep into the realm of complex oxide epitaxial thin films, a class of materials holding promises that have the potential to reshape our technological landscape.
Complex Oxides
Why Complex Oxides?
Complex oxides, particularly those based on transition metals, are a treasure trove of multifaceted properties. These materials can exhibit a rich variety of physical behaviors, from ferroelectricity and magnetism to superconductivity and unconventional transport. Such diverse characteristics stem from the interplay of charge, spin, lattice, and orbital degrees of freedom at the atomic level. It's no wonder that these materials have garnered attention for their potential to revolutionize everything from computing to energy storage.

Elevating the Paradigm
But we're not just about understanding these properties; we're about mastery. Our research is not confined to merely tuning the inherent traits of these oxides. Instead, we embark on a more audacious journey — controlling these materials at the single atomic layer level. This meticulous level of manipulation allows us to envision and create materials and functionalities that have never before been realized in the world. We are pushing the boundaries of what's possible by synthesizing new forms, conjuring up unprecedented properties, and harnessing their potential in next-generation applications.
Diverse Frontiers
Diverse Frontiers: Ferro- & Flexoelectricity to Spin-orbitronics & Superconductivity
Our exploration begins with the intriguing world of ferroelectricity. These materials, possessing spontaneous electric polarization that can be reversed by an external electric field, hold great potential in non-volatile memory devices and advanced sensing applications.

Venturing further, we delve into the realm of flexoelectricity. This intriguing phenomenon arises when mechanical asymmetries produce electric polarization. Such properties pave the way for innovative applications in energy harvesting and nano-electromechanical systems.

One of our pivotal research avenues is spin-orbitronics. By understanding and controlling the complex interplay between an electron's spin and its orbital motion, we uncover groundbreaking prospects in data storage and quantum computing. Harnessing this synergy in our epitaxial films might be the key to realizing ultrafast, low-energy electronics, bridging the present to a quantum future.

Lastly, our passion for understanding and utilizing unique properties has led us to investigate superconductivity in complex oxides. The promise of zero electrical resistance at remarkably high temperatures not only challenges our understanding of condensed matter physics but also opens doors to revolutionary applications like quantum computing, efficient energy transmission, and next-generation magnetic levitation transport.
Through each of these frontiers, we aim not just to understand, but to redefine the boundaries of what's possible in condensed matter physics & materials science.
Vision
A Vision for Tomorrow
At ACOL, we believe that the materials of tomorrow will be defined by our ability to craft, control, and comprehend them at atomic precisions. Our investigations into complex oxide epitaxial thin films are not just about exploring new frontiers; they're about creating them. We invite you to join us on this exhilarating journey as we sculpt the future, one atomic layer at a time.

We read proteins and chemical reactions, one molecule at a time.
DISCOVER WHAT MOVES LIFE
We develop new ways to observe, understand, and control molecular dynamics
Research
Unlimited Possibilities.

RESEARCH THEMES
Chemistry + Biology in SPACE and TIME
Chemical and biological processes are fundamentally governed by their organization in space and time. We go beyond conventional kinetic models to quantify how spatiotemporal patterns emerge from molecular interactions. Our work establishes a quantitative framework linking macroscopic reaction behavior with subcellular signaling dynamics.

Membrane Protein Interactions x Cell Signals
Cellular signaling is initiated by membrane receptor activation driven by protein–protein interactions.We study how these interactions encode and propagate multidimensional information across molecular, cellular, and system levels. Our goal is to uncover the principles that connect receptor dynamics to cellular decision-making and phenotype.

Nanomedicine
We develop new therapeutic strategies based on nanoparticles, antibodies, proteins, and oligonucleotides.
Our approach focuses on precise control of biological systems through engineered nanoscale interactions.We aim to establish programmable platforms for targeted intervention in complex diseases.

TOOLS AND APPROACHES
Nanoparticle Chemistry
Proteins
We design and synthesize functional nanomaterials with controlled composition, structure, and surface chemistry. These nanoprobes enable precise interaction with biological systems at the molecular and cellular levels. They serve as both sensors and actuators for probing and manipulating complex biological environments.

Advanced Microscopy
Signaling
We develop and apply high-resolution optical imaging techniques to observe biological processes in real time. Our platforms enable single-molecule and live-cell measurements with high spatial and temporal precision. These approaches allow direct quantification of dynamic behaviors that are inaccessible by ensemble methods.

AI-based Prediction
Microscope
We employ machine learning and statistical modeling to analyze complex and high-dimensional datasets. Our methods extract hidden patterns and infer underlying mechanisms from single-molecule and cellular data. This enables predictive understanding and quantitative interpretation of biological systems.

Cell + Protein Engineering
AI
We use genetic and biochemical tools to engineer proteins and cellular systems with defined functions. These approaches allow precise control over molecular interactions and signaling pathways. They provide a platform to test mechanistic hypotheses and design functional biological systems.

intro.text:
Chemical-Based Aging Research Lab
Chang Lab aims to develop live senescent cell probes and control the aging process, by chemical or photodynamic approach.

DOFL compounds are generated by combinatorial modification of organic fluorescent scaffolds, where simple building blocks can be assembled with the aim of creating diverse compounds. The design and preparation of DOFL focus on exploring the diverse chemical space directly around a fluorescent scaffold. This approach provides some advantages in the development of bioimaging probes since it can be applied without knowledge about the target molecule and an additional reporter is not required for the visualization of the probes. Therefore, DOFLA depends entirely on the structural diversity of the fluorescence library empowered by the unbiased evaluation of compounds to identify target-selective fluorescent probes. DOFL derived from fluorescence scaffolds such as rosamine, BODIPY, chalcone, and xanthone covers a very wide range of chemical space and fluorescence spectra (400−800 nm).
We have developed more than 30 livel cell probes and figured out the unique mechanisms. HOLD (Holding-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes have binding biomarkers on or inside the target cells. The biomarkers can be proteins, carbohydrates, DNA, etc. GOLD (Gating-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes selectively enter or are excluded from target cells through specific transporters. GOLD probes are substrates of transporters, whose cell-type-specific accumulation is majorly dependent on transporters. LOLD (Lipid-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes are loaded on the target cell membrane through a kinetically controlled membrane fusion. MOLD (Metabolism-Oriented Live-cell Distinction) probes selectively stain target cells through a unique metabolism.

intro.text:
Welcome to SMART Lab
SMART 연구실의 목표는 인류의 건강한 삶에 기여하는 지속가능한 친환경기술을 개발하는 것입니다. 이를 위하여 태양에너지 기반의 해수담수화 기술, 공기 중 수분을 이용한 에너지 하베스팅 기술, 고효율의 광물탄산화 기술, 나노셀룰로오스 기반의 초경량강화 소재를 개발하고 있습니다. 본 연구실 연구의 가장 큰 특징은 바이오, 환경, 소재, 물리, 화학, 기계, 화공 등 과학과 공학을 아우르는 융합연구에 있습니다. 인류의 건강한 삶에 기여하는 지속가능한 기술 개발에 열정과 관심 있는 학생들의 지원을 환영합니다.
The goal of the SMART Laboratory is to develop sustainable technologies that contribute to the healthy life of mankind. To this end, we are developing seawater desalination technology based on solar energy, energy harvesting technology utilizing moisture, highly efficient carbon mineralization technology, and ultralight super-materials based on nanocellulose. The most distinctive feature of the researches in our laboratory is the convergence research that encompasses science and engineering such as bio, environment, materials, physics, chemistry, mechanical engineering, and chemical engineering. We welcome students who are passionate and interested in developing sustainable technologies that contribute to the healthy life of mankind.
특정 외부 자극에 응답하는 특별한 특성을 가지면서도 매우 작은 크기를 가지는 지능형 나노물질은 기존의 과학적, 공학적 한계를 극복할 수 있는 잠재력을 가지고 있습니다. 우리 연구실은 지능형 나노입자를 기반으로 감염성 질병의 진단을 위한 스마트 디바이스의 개발과 지능형 나노섬유를 기반으로 미래 산업을 주도할 첨단 소재 기술을 개발하고 있습니다.
환경과 인류가 공존하면서도 미래산업이 발전하기 위해서는 지속 가능한 친환경기술의 개발이 필수적입니다. 우리 연구실에서는 태양에너지, 해수 및 대기 중의 수분 등과 같은 풍부한 천연자원을 이용하거나 버려지는 에너지를 수집하는 다양한 에너지 하베스팅 기술을 개발하고 있습니다. 또한, 태양에너지 기반의 친환경 해수담수화 및 셀룰로오스 기반의 첨단 미래소재 등 인류의 미래를 위한 탄소중립화 기술개발을 선도하고 있습니다.

Sustainable Materials
Magnetic nanoparticle cluster (MNC)
자성 나노입자 클러스터(Magnetic Nanoparticle Cluster ; MNC)는 산화철 나노입자로 이루어진 수백 나노미터 크기의 클러스터로 초상자성과 높은 자화도를 가지는 특징이 있습니다. MNC의 표면은 쉽게 개질 가능하기 때문에 고분자, 항체를 비롯한 다양한 물질들을 부착할 수 있습니다. 따라서 적절한 capture probe를 이용한다면 자석을 이용해 원하는 타겟을 빠르고 간단하게 분…
Nanocellulose
셀룰로오스는 자연에서 얻을 수 있는 가장 풍부한 고분자 물질입니다. 셀룰로오스에서 분리한 나노셀룰로오스(nanocellulose)는 직경이 2 – 10 nm 의 아주 얇은 입자 또는 섬유로, 기존 소재들의 한계를 뛰어넘을 수 있는 잠재력을 지니고 있습니다. 나노셀룰로오스는 인장탄성계수(tensile strength)가 강철과 비견될 정도이며, 생분해성, 초경량성, 투명성 등의 장점 덕분에 다양한 분야에 응용될 수 있습니다. …
Electrospun nanofiber
전기방사 (Electrospinning) 는 전기력을 이용하여 고분자 용액 또는 용융물을 수백 나노미터 직경으로 뽑아내는 섬유 생산 방법입니다. 나노섬유의 구조, 크기, 기공도 등의 조절이 용이하기 때문에 의공학, 산업적 측면에서 가치가 높은 기술입니다. SMART Lab에서는 지능형 나노물질을 나노섬유의 표면에 코팅하거나, 섬유 내부에 혼합하여 특별한 특성을 지니는 기능성 나노섬유를 개발하…
Smart filter
기존 필터는 공기 중 유해물질을 차단하거나 액상에서 혼합액을 분리하는 등 여과기 역할을 했습니다. 그러나, 코로나19로 인해 바이오 에어로졸의 전파를 막기위한 필터의 수요가 증가하면서 단순한 여과 기능 향상뿐만 아니라 친환경, 항균성 소재 기반의 기능성 필터 개발이 요구되고 있습니다. SMART Lab에서는 생분해성 고분자 소재 기반 섬유, solvent-free 섬유 등 인체에 무해하며 친환경적인 섬유 개발에 대한 연구가 진행 중이며, 성능 향상을 위해 위 섬…

Renewable Technologies
Solar steam generation (SSG)
아직도 전세계에서는 수십억 명의 인류가 물 부족을 겪고 있으나 기존의 해수담수화 기술은 설비 비용과 에너지 소모로 인해 한계가 있는 실정입니다. Solar steam generation (SSG) 는 지구상에 풍부하고 지속가능한 태양에너지를 활용하여 추가적인 에너지 투입 없이 깨끗한 물을 얻는 해수담수화 및 수질정화 기술입니다. 효율적인 SSG를 위해서는 에너지의 흡수 및 집중화, 물 수송, 단열, 표면적, 내염성 등 다양한 요소가 고려되어야 하기 때문에 물질 및 구조의 측면에서 창의적인 연구가 활발히 진행되고 있습니다…
Moisture-induced power generation (MPG)
에너지난 시대에 일상에서 버려지는 각종 에너지를 수거해 재활용하는 에너지 수확 (energy harvesting) 기술 개발이 활발해지고 있습니다. 그 중, Moisture-induced power generation (MPG)은 대기 중의 수분을 흡수하여 전기를 발생하는 기술로 물의 흡착 및 확산 등 자발적인 표면 현상에 의해 발전되어, 높은 에너지 전환율로 각광 받고 있는 친환경 발전기입니다. 지속 가능하고 효율적인 수분 발전기를 개발하기 위해서 자발적인 수분 흡수, 수분에 의한 이온의 농도 구배, 이…
Carbon mineralization
전세계에서 매년 과량의 CO2가 배출되고 있습니다. 이에 대한 해결책으로 지층 혹은 해양에 탄소를 저장하는 기술이 거론되고 있으나, 각각 부족한 용량과 환경적인 문제로 인해 심층적인 개발에 어려움을 겪고 있습니다. 광물 탄산화 (carbon mineralization)은 칼슘, 마그네슘 등과 이산화탄소를 반응시켜 불용성 탄산염을 만드는 기술로써, 생성물은 열역학적으로 안정하고 다양한 분야에 활용할 수 있다는 장점이 있습니다. 효율적인 광물 탄산화를 위해서는 반응속도를 높일 수 있는 촉진제가 필요하지만 안정성 및 회수에 대한 한계점이…

intro.text:
Ionic Cluster
Structures of Biomolecules

IMS-MS machine Development
All-Mass Spectrometry Thing
Ionic Cluster
We investigates ionic clusters, assemblies of ions and molecules, using mass spectrometry. We couple electrospray ionization (ESI) with ion mobility spectrometry–mass spectrometry (IMS–MS) to generate weakly bound ionic clusters in the gas phase and to quantify collision cross sections (CCS), which provide conformational information of ionic clusters. By integrating CID/MSⁿ experiments with quantum-chemical calculations (DFT) and trajectory-method CCS predictions, we predict the structures and thermodynamic stability of ionic clusters and host-guest complexes including alkali halide ions, amino acids, saccharides, and N, O-donor ligands. Together, these measurements provide reproducible structural constraints that inform electrolyte design, ion transport, and supramolecular assembly across solution, interfacial, and gas-phase regimes.

Ionic Cluster
We investigates ionic clusters, assemblies of ions and molecules, using mass spectrometry. We couple electrospray ionization (ESI) with ion mobility spectrometry–mass spectrometry (IMS–MS) to generate weakly bound ionic clusters in the gas phase and to quantify collision cross sections (CCS), which provide conformational information of ionic clusters. By integrating CID/MSⁿ experiments with quantum-chemical calculations (DFT) and trajectory-method CCS predictions, we predict the structures and thermodynamic stability of ionic clusters and host-guest complexes including alkali halide ions, amino acids, saccharides, and N, O-donor ligands. Together, these measurements provide reproducible structural constraints that inform electrolyte design, ion transport, and supramolecular assembly across solution, interfacial, and gas-phase regimes.

Structures of Biomolecules
The structure–function relationship is a fundamental principle underlying all biological systems. Consequently, the study of the molecular structures of biological macromolecules, with a particular focus on proteins and nucleic acids, is essential for comprehending biological processes.
Since the 20th century, the development of mass spectrometry (MS) has encompassed techniques such as electrospray ionisation (ESI) and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation (MALDI), enabling the transfer of delicate biomolecules from solution into the gas phase.
In our research, we couple MS with ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) to obtain additional information called the collision cross section (CCS), which reflects the surface area of biomolecules. This CCS has been demonstrated to serve as an indicator of structural preservation or unfolding. By employing it as an index, it is possible to interpret structural stability and features that were previously inaccessible.

Charged Droplet Chemistry
Charged micro- and nano droplets generated in electrospray ionization (ESI) form during solvent evaporation. These charged droplets possess large surface-to-volume ratios, high surface charge densities, and strong interfacial electric fields that create pH/composition gradients, enrich reactants, and accelerate interfacial chemistry. As a result, product distributions may deviate from bulk behavior in some systems—for example, regio-, chemo-, or enantioselectivity can shift, and protomer/tautomer ratios may differ. We use ESI–ion mobility–mass spectrometry, which resolves isomeric and protomeric ions by their collisional cross sections, together with tandem mass spectrometry to obtain structure-specific fragments, and we interpret these measurements using density functional theory to propose and evaluate candidate structures and protonation sites. Studying chemical behavior in charged droplets matters because it can change the signals we measure and sometimes allows reactions that don’t appear in bulk; measuring these effects makes ESI–MS results more trustworthy and helps us control selectivity.

IMS-MS machine Development
We have been developing SLIM(Structures for Lossless Ion manipulations)-based, high-resolution ion mobility platforms that enable IMS-photo-IMS experiments for structure-selective analysis in the gas phase. Using a few meter-long ion mobility paths and switching components, ions with specific strcutrues are captured in the trap region. A tunable laser introduced between the tandem IM stages drives wavelength-dependent photodissociation and photoisomerization, creating diagnostically useful product ions. By reinjecting photo-induced products into a second IM separation and coupling to MS, we obtain accurate collision cross sections, isomer-resolved photochemistry, and unambiguous connectivity between precursor and product ions. This workflow clarifies 3D structures and dynamics of biomolecular ions, ionic clusters, and reactive intermediates that are difficult to resolve by IM–MS alone.

All-Mass Spectrometry Thing
We also pursue a broad range of mass spectrometry–based studies. These include developing new analytical methods to observe and quantify large clusters such as nanoclusters and quantum dots(QD). Photochemistry-mass spectrometry enables characterizing photoisomeric species. We are doing comprehensive mass spectrometric analyses and structure elucidation of diverse organic/inorganic molecules and clusters.

Mobile CMOS Image Sensor

Advanced Sensing
The PIXEL LAB at POSTECH designs high-performance image sensors that overcome conventional limits by integrating advanced materials and device technologies, including quantum dots, thin-film transistors (TFT/TFPD), and perovskites. Through these innovations, we develop next-generation 2D and 3D imaging solutions that extend capabilities beyond visible light into the short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectrum.
SWIR Image Sensor
Thin-Film Based 4T PPD
Readout Circuit (ROIC) Design
Halide Perovskite Image Sensor

obile CMOS Image Sensor
The PIXEL LAB specializes in state-of-the-art CMOS Image Sensor (CIS) pixel design and analysis, leveraging advanced TCAD and FDTD simulations for precise electrical and optical device optimization. Through meticulous modeling and modular analysis, we advance the core technologies that drive the next generation of high-resolution, intelligent smartphone camera sensors.

Pixel Architecture & Device Modeling
Noise & Dark Current Characterization
Optical Analysis

Single Photon Avalanche Diode
The PIXEL LAB designs single-photon avalanche diodes that form their multiplication field by field-line crowding around a small hemispherical cathode, creating a spherically uniform field peak that funnels electrons from the entire absorption volume and decouples detection efficiency from pixel pitch. This delivers state-of-the-art NIR sensitivity and LiDAR-grade timing on a backside-illuminated CMOS platform. Building on it, we move image processing into the sensor itself, coupling the SPAD’s pulse output to a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron model that encodes 2D and edge images purely as spike counts.

NIR-Enhanced Silicon SPAD for Time-of-Flight Imaging
On-Chip Image Processing with SPAD Image Sensors

AI Based Device Design
The research on AI Device Design at Pixel Lab focuses on innovating next-generation semiconductor device analysis and inverse design by replacing conventional, time-consuming TCAD/FDTD simulations with fast, AI-based surrogate models. This approach leverages differentiable solvers and JAX-based automatic differentiation to enable an efficient inverse design loop, ultimately enhancing semiconductor device performance.

intro.text:
Full research statementopen
Stochastically modeled reaction networks: A biochemical system is described with a graphical configuration called a reaction network. These graphical configurations are used to model broad classes of interaction systems including signaling systems, viral infections, metabolism, neuronal networks, population models, etc. One of the most challenging issues systems biologists face is the extraordinarily complicated structure of a system. Thus, characterizing the system structure is a major open question in the field as the structure induces emergent phenotypes and behaviors of the system’s dynamics.
To find other network characterization, my colleges and I have used a hierarchical structure of given reactions, so-called `generalized tier-structures’, to discover new network conditions guaranteeing that the associated stochastic process admits a stationary distribution. Those network conditions can be satisfied in more realistic models such as i) fully-open bimolecular systems with a single weakly reversible component, ii) bimolecular system with dimerization of each species, or iii) bimolecular system with a single linkage class including all the dimers or monomers [1, 4, 5]. Importantly, the stability holds regardless of the choice of system parameters for the model, which are typically unknown in practice.
Absolutely robust controllers: By using the long-term stability of reaction systems, my colleague and I constructed absolutely robust controllers that can control the distribution of molecular counts in a given stochastic system. As opposed to controlling deterministic models, we have additional control goals for stochastic models because it is important to control not only the mean expression level but also its variance (i.e. noise) and ideally the full probability distribution of the target species. In [3], we showed that if some stability condition is met, the target species in the controlled system follows a Poisson distribution centered at a user-defined value. Since the control species can suffer from complete extinction, we set high initial abundance for the control species. As the control species has the higher order of copy numbers, we have used multi-scaling analysis to prove the long-term stability of the controlled system and in turn verified controllability of our synthetic circuit.
Not only the stochastic models but also the target species in a deterministic model can be controlled with our controller as its concentration is driven to the desired steady state value. We also have emphasized that the controlled system under both deterministic and stochastic settings is resistant to external disturbances such as parameter changes and additional in- and out-flows. This property is known as robust perfect adaptation, which is a highly desirable goal in control theory.
Computing rare event probabilities via network modifications: We are often interested in rare events of a stochastic model such as the extinction of diseases. Stochastic simulation algorithms including Gillespie’s algorithm have been typically employed to estimate the probability distribution of a Markov process. However, when the target event rarely occurs, significantly long simulations may be required to sample enough trajectories to estimate the distribution of the system. Alternatively, the chemical master equation, which is a system of ordinary differential equations, can be utilized to compute the rare event probability. However, it can suffer from dimensionality as a stochastic system often admits infinitely many states.
In [8], we proposed a new network modification method that automatically truncates the state-space. The modified network composed of `slack reactants’ added to a given network has approximately the same dynamic as the original system. We proved that the modified system converges to the original system as the size of truncation increases. We also provided the application of our theoretical frameworks with practical reaction network models.
Evidence of cooperativity in in vivo immune cells: I collaborated with biologists in Alexander Hoffmann’s lab to investigate mechanistic principles and biophysical parameters that allow SDTF binding to generate distinct epigenomes in living organs, in the context of pathogen responses. By utilizing experimental measurements of location-specific nucleosome counts with ATAC-seq, a next-generation sequencing technology, we detected from the experimental data evidence of cooperativity in nucleosome unwrapping steps. We then investigated the influence of SDTF-binding location on nucleosome eviction and estimated the system parameters using reverse engineering. Our efforts provide rules governing nucleosome dynamics in vivo that can predict how nucleosomes respond to SDTF activation at specific genomic locations to produce epigenomic alterations during inflammation.
Size control mechanism of chlamydia in a host cell: I am currently supported by an NIH research grant for researching the size-control mechanism of chlamydia. Chlamydia is a bacteria causing widespread human diseases by infecting eukaryotic host cells. Unlike the well-known cell division mechanism that typically maintains the size of each cell, the average size of chlamydia decreases during its developmental cycle. The size-control mechanism was proposed as the replicating forms (RB) become progressively smaller through repeated cycles of replication and convert into the infectious forms (EB) only below a size threshold (Lee et. al. 2018). Our current project is to test our hypothesis experimentally and mathematically. We use a branching process to describe division and conversion of chlamydia and to study the size-control mechanism.
Effect of intrinsic noise in biological systems: A stochastic system is not necessarily understood as a process fluctuating around the trajectory of the deterministic counterpart. Many examples are known to have a discrepancy between stochastic and deterministic modeling. For instance, cell polarity can be induced by oscillations in the stochastic system, while it is not found for comparable parameters in the deterministic case [2]. Moreover, a stochastic model can admit multi-peaks in the long-term distribution, which can represent multiple potential phenotypes in a single cell system, while the deterministic counterpart admits only a single steady state. Although such an effect of intrinsic noise was proposed in many systems, a rigorous verification was not often provided. In [7], we proved stability and finite moment conditions for a class of autocatalytic systems. We also verified the effect of the intrinsic noise in the system by finding that the stationary distribution of the autocatalytic systems is Dirichlet-multinomial distribution, which has multi-peaks when the system volume is small. This multimodality is not realized in the deterministic counterpart that has a single stable steady state.
Biochemical network inference: The structure of biochemical networks and the associated parameters are typically unknown in practice. Many theoretical and computational methods such as Bayesian inference and machine-learning tools were proposed to infer the system parameters and the underlying network structures. However, many of the previous works have not answered a critical question: can the underlying model be identifiable with given data? It is possible that two different systems have the same dynamical profiles, meaning that the true model cannot be uniquely identified with given dynamical data. This indicates that the identifiability of the given system must be verified prior to the inference of a network structure and parameter estimation. In [9], I quantified the amount of transition rate information needed to uniquely identify the underlying biochemical network. I also proved that the time evolution of stochastic dynamics can be used to infer the hidden network structure, while information of deterministic dynamics may not uniquely characterize the network structure. We also proposed an algorithm that enables us to infer the underlying reaction network and the associated parameters with the transition data of a given continuous time Markov chain.
9. German Enciso, Radek Erban and Jinsu Kim, Identifiability of Stochastically Modelled Reaction Networks, accepted to European Journal of Applied Mathematics, 2020.
8. Jinsu Kim, Jason Dark, German Enciso and Suzanne Sindi, Slack Reactants: A State-Space Truncation Framework to Estimate Quantitative Behavior of the Chemical Master Equation, J. Chem. Phys. 153, 054117 (2020)
7. Enrico Bibbona, Jinsu Kim and Carsten Wiuf, Stationary distributions of systems with Discreteness Induced Transitions, J. R. Soc. Interface. 1720200243, 2020.
6. German Enciso and Jinsu Kim, Accuracy of Multiscale Reduction for Stochastic Reaction Systems, submitted, 2019.
5. David F. Anderson, Daniele Cappelletti, Jinsu Kim, and Tung Nguyen, Tier structure of strongly endotactic reaction networks, to appear in Stochastic Processes and their Applications .
4. David F. Anderson, Daniele Cappelletti and Jinsu Kim, Stochastically modeled weakly reversible reaction networks with a single linkage class, Journal of Applied Probability. 57(3), 792-810, 2020
3. Jinsu Kim and German Enciso , Absolutely Robust Controllers for Stochastic Chemical Reaction Networks, J. R. Soc. Interface. 17: 20200031, 2020.
2. German Enciso and Jinsu Kim, Embracing noise in chemical reaction networks, Bull Math Biol, 81, 1261–1267, 2019.
1. David F. Anderson and Jinsu Kim, Some network conditions for positive recurrence of stochastically modeled reaction networks, SIAM Journal of Applied Mathematics, 78(5), 2692-2713, 2018.

We develop integrated frameworks where biological signals meet physical embodiments. Our goal is to create next-generation systems that seamlessly synthesize human intelligence, robotic mechanics, and AI.
Bridging the Gap Between Brain, Robots, and Artificial Intelligence
The BRAINs Lab (Brain–Robot–Artificial Intelligence Integrated System Laboratory) at POSTECH explores the intersection of neuroscience, robotics, and artificial intelligence. We unite these fields to decode how the brain works and to design its abilities in robots.

Through an integrated “brain–robot–AI” approach, we develop next-generation reinforcement learning algorithms, bio-inspired robots, and advanced neural probe systems — creating technologies that explore the deepest mysteries of the brain and redefine how humans and machines interact.

Our Core Research Areas
01
Brain-Computer Interface
We design advanced neural probe systems and interfaces that record and decode neural activity, building reliable bridges between the brain and external machines — to understand how the brain works and to restore or extend its abilities.

We develop advanced neural probe systems and brain–computer interfaces that record and decode neural activity, forming a reliable bridge between the brain and external computers.
Our research spans implantable and flexible neural electrodes, high-density neural recording, and real-time decoding of neural signals. By combining neuroscience, soft materials, and device engineering, we pursue stable, long-term, and minimally invasive interfacing with neural tissue.
Through these efforts, we aim to advance neuroprosthetics, brain-controlled robotics, and the restoration and extension of human sensory and motor function.
02
Bio-Inspired Micro-Robotics
Drawing on principles observed in living organisms, we develop bio-inspired and soft micro-robots that move, sense, and adapt within complex physical environments, translating the intelligence of biological systems into engineered machines.

We design and fabricate bio-inspired micro-robots that leverage principles from biological systems to achieve efficient movement and functionality at micro/nano scales.
Our research focuses on smart materials, soft micro-actuators, and magnetic/optical propulsion methods to enable precise control in dynamic and complex environments.
Through these advances, we aim to transform biomedical applications, including targeted drug delivery, minimally invasive surgery, and cellular-level tissue manipulation.
03
AI-Integrated Physical Convergence
We build next-generation reinforcement learning algorithms and physical-AI systems that unite perception, learning, and action — seamlessly synthesizing human intelligence, robotics, and AI to bridge the gap between the physical and digital worlds.

We pioneer AI-integrated physital (physical + digital) systems that bridge physical hardware with digital intelligence for real-time sensing, analysis, and execution.
Our research focuses on embedded machine learning, physical AI architectures, and intelligent sensor-actuator networks to enable autonomous adaptation and interactive control.
Through this convergence, we aim to transform smart environments, human-machine interaction, and next-generation autonomous engineering solutions.

Use soft things to solve hard problems
The overall aim of our research is to understand and control the structure and dynamics of soft matter at interfaces in dimensions ranging from nano- to macroscale and engineer new functional materials. A key aspect of our research is the preparation of well-defined molecules, materials, emulsions and surfaces, which leads to desired function.
Interface engineering
Microfluidics
Encryption and Display
Artificial cell
Healthcare and Sustainability
Wetting
The ability to control surface wettability plays an important role in many applications, from antifogging and self-cleaning surfaces to enhancing condensation. By manipulating surface energy and microstructural design, we aim to develop hydrophilic and hydrophobic surfaces tailored for specific functionalities. These designs enable the effective management of water droplets, leading to advancements in antifogging coatings, liquid-repellent surfaces, and more.
Hydrogel
Hydrogels, known for their high water content and tunable mechanical properties, serve as versatile materials in designing functional interfaces. We explore their applications in creating antifogging layers, responsive coatings, and soft actuators. By adjusting chemical compositions and crosslinking densities, we tailor hydrogels to exhibit specific responses to environmental stimuli such as humidity and temperature, broadening their utility across diverse fields.
Micropatterning
Micropatterning techniques enable precise spatial control over material properties and surface functionalities. Using advanced methods like lithography, we fabricate microstructured surfaces that enhance optical transparency, mechanical stability, and environmental resilience. These patterned surfaces find applications in flexible electronics, optical devices, and multifunctional coatings that integrate hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions seamlessly.
Nanofibers
Electrospinning is a versatile technique for generating continuous nanofibers with high surface area, enhancing the wettability of materials. These nanofiber matrices exhibit a high surface area, interconnected pores, and thin permeation paths. By exploiting these properties, we aim to develop high-performance membranes with superior permeability for various applications.

We explore their applications in creating antifogging layers, responsive coatings, and soft actuators. By adjusting chemical compositions and crosslinking densities, we tailor hydrogels to exhibit specific responses to environmental stimuli such as humidity and temperature, broadening their utility across diverse fields.

Using advanced methods like lithography, we fabricate microstructured surfaces that enhance optical transparency, mechanical stability, and environmental resilience. These patterned surfaces find applications in flexible electronics, optical devices, and multifunctional coatings that integrate hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions seamlessly.
Nanofibers
Electrospinning is a versatile technique for generating continuous nanofibers with high surface area, enhancing the wettability of materials. These nanofiber matrices exhibit a high surface area, interconnected pores, and thin permeation paths. By exploiting these properties, we aim to develop high-performance membranes with superior permeability for various applications.

Microfluidics
Multi-phase Emulsion
Multi-phase emulsions, with their intricate structures, offer a platform where composition and structure can be precisely regulated through advanced microfluidic techniques. These systems enable independent control of inner and outer droplets, making them highly suitable for applications in sophisticated material encapsulation and controlled release. By leveraging diverse interfacial-active materials such as particles and surfactants, we fine-tune the physical and chemical properties of the emulsion shell, enabling selective material release and precise control over phase transitions. These emulsions are particularly promising as drug delivery systems and as microenvironments for catalytic reactions.
Vesicles and Microcapsules
Droplet microfluidics offers precise and simultaneous control over flow conditions, enabling the production of multiple emulsion droplets with tunable composition and structure. These droplets serve as versatile templates for incorporating unique functionalities tailored to specific applications. For instance, we utilize temperature-responsive materials in Janus particles to enhance emulsion stability while enabling on-demand coalescence. Additionally, we design shell membranes for double emulsion droplets and microcapsules to regulate material transport and utilize them in advanced smart release systems.
3D Printing
3D printing presents a groundbreaking approach to fabricating microfluidic devices, enabling the construction of microchannels with complex geometries. This technique allows for controlled outputs on the scale of tens of micrometers, facilitating the creation of fully three-dimensional channels and intricate surface modifications. Compared to traditional microfluidic fabrication methods, 3D printing enhances parallelization, screening capabilities, and mass production efficiency. It is widely applicable to various liquid-based processes, including micromixers, solution exchange, filtration, and droplet microfluidics.
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is an indispensable tool for numerically analyzing and predicting fluid behavior, enabling the study of complex flow phenomena as well as thermal and mass transport across multiple scales. Our research leverages high-performance computing and diverse numerical methods to address challenges in fluid mechanics and uncover transformative insights. In real-world systems, multifaceted flow regimes—spanning laminar, turbulent, single-phase, and multiphase flows—frequently coexist. Through CFD simulations, we replicate these intricate dynamics with high fidelity, providing insights that are difficult to achieve experimentally. This approach improves predictive model reliability for design parameters such as flow distribution, pressure drops, temperature gradients, and concentration profiles. CFD also facilitates the transition from laboratory or pilot-scale verifications to full-scale commercial implementations by identifying and addressing latent flow issues, optimizing energy utilization, reaction efficiency, and production throughput. By integrating CFD, we aim to pioneer efficient and visionary fluid engineering solutions and foster cross-disciplinary innovation.

Encryption and Display
Optical encryption technologies and dynamic displays are revolutionized through the integration of wettability patterning and structural color. By leveraging multi-level wettability systems and programmable photoreactive polymers, we create advanced anti-counterfeiting measures and transformational full-color devices. These innovations offer unprecedented control over color and information display, paving the way for secure, interactive, and visually striking solutions in information security and consumer electronics.

Artificial Cell
Cells perform a variety of complex biochemical reactions orchestrated in space and time. These features have driven advancements in biotechnology, biosensors, biogenesis, bioreactors, and drug delivery. To replicate and understand these cellular functions, we develop artificial cell-like vesicles that mimic key cellular hallmarks, including metabolic pathways, material transport, and protein synthesis. Using droplet microfluidics, we produce monodisperse vesicles with highly efficient encapsulation and compartmentalization of biomolecules. These artificial cells provide a new avenue for designing responsive and programmable protocell systems through a bottom-up approach.

Healthcare and Sustainability
Conventional polymer materials are typically incinerated or landfilled, causing significant environmental and ecological harm. To address this, biodegradable materials have garnered considerable attention due to their ability to decompose into water and carbon dioxide through microbial activity. This environmentally friendly process eliminates the need for external energy inputs. Our research focuses on designing functional interfaces using these biodegradable materials, ensuring sustainability and contributing to environmental preservation.

intro.text:
Research Focus
Model Compression
Model Compression As AI models become larger and more computationally demanding, compression is essential for making them practical and sustainable. We develop optimization methods that reduce training and inference costs while preserving model performance. Our work focuses on extreme compression across the AI model lifecycle.
more
🔍

Extreme Sparsity (EMNLP '26, ICLR '26, ICML '25 Spotlight, EMNLP '24)
We push the limits of LLM sparsity through advanced optimization frameworks such as ADMM, aiming for robust generalization even at extreme compression levels.
Joint Compression
We develop unified frameworks that integrate pruning, quantization, and distillation to reduce error accumulation and preserve core model capabilities, including reasoning, in highly compressed states.
Distributed Training
Distributed Training The shift toward massive-scale models has made distributed training essential for workloads that no single machine can support. From an optimization perspective, the key challenge is maintaining efficiency while managing the overhead of communication between devices. Our research develops robust algorithms for decentralized and high-latency training environments.
more
🔍

Communication-Efficient Training (NeurIPS '26 WS)
We design methods that reduce the heavy data-sharing requirements of distributed training through information compression, reduced synchronization, and zeroth-order optimization.
Asynchronous Training (NeurIPS '26, ICML '26)
We create algorithms that allow devices to work independently and reduce waiting time, with a focus on correcting errors caused by slightly outdated information.
Device-Heterogeneous Training
We develop adaptive strategies for imbalanced computational resources across devices, aiming for consistent global convergence despite variations in hardware performance.
Advanced Optimization
Advanced Optimization Optimization has long been a source of crucial ideas that drastically enhance all corners of deep neural network training, and many of its most impactful questions remain open. Our research investigates these questions and develops optimization principles and algorithms for modern deep learning systems.
more
🔍

Optimization for Generalization (UAI '25, ICML '25)
We study the role of loss landscape curvature in generalization and develop flatness-oriented optimization strategies with both theoretical advantages and scalability for modern deep neural networks.
Zeroth-Order Optimization for Black-Box Model Training (ICLR '25)
We develop methods that operate without direct gradient access, motivated by settings such as proprietary model APIs and decentralized learning systems where gradients are unavailable.

We aim to uncover the mechanisms that regulate cell identity, tissue regeneration, aging, and organ development, using both in vivo models and organoid systems.

Lab Philosophy
"We prioritize questions over techniques."
"We value results that challenge our own models."
"We believe small perturbations can reveal governing principles of complex biological systems."
Classic regenerative biology focuses on stem cell behavior in isolation.
We ask instead:
When a subset of cells changes state, how does that perturb local niches, remodel tissue networks, and amplify regenerative responses?
Our recent work demonstrates that partial reprogramming can propagate widespread repair characteristics across cell types and environments.
Featured Publications
Nature Communications (2026)
We show that mosaic partial cellular reprogramming not only alters targeted epithelial cells but also remodels neighboring microenvironments and immune networks, leading to enhanced wound healing and tissue regeneration.

Transition-metal-catalyzed chemo-, regio-, and stereoselective
Our research aims to discover, develop and understand new transition-metal-catalyzed organic transformations of broad interest to organic synthesis. We are particularly interested in the design of efficient catalytic systems that operate through uncommon modes of activation and which will result in a rapid increase in molecular complexity.
The following topics will be investigated in my group:
We have observed that α-borylcarbanion, generated in situ from the reaction of 1,1-diborylalkane with an alkoxide base, could facilitate an unprecedented base-promoted deborylative alkylation of N-heteroarenes. The reaction proceeds efficiently for a wide range of N-heteroarenes and 1,1-diborylalkanes with excellent regioselectivity. The reaction also can be applied for the direct introduction of a methyl group to 9-O-methylquinine N-oxide, thus it can serve as a powerful method for late-stage functionalization. Moreover, a new transition-metal-free borylation of aryl and vinyl halides using 1,1-diborylalkanes as boron sources is also developed. In this transformation one of the boron groups from 1,1-diborylalkanes is selectively transferred to aryl and vinyl halides in the presence of sodium tert-butoxide as the only activator to form organoboronate esters. Under the developed borylation conditions, a broad range of organohalides are borylated with excellent chemoselectivity and functional group compatibility, thus offering a rare example of a transition-metal-free borylation protocol.
We have observed that the chemoselective transmetalation of 1,1-diborylalkanes with copper catalyst can be achieved in the presence of alkoxide base. The generated a-borylalkylcopper species underwent a highly chemo- and diastereoselective alkylation of N–tert-butanesulfinyl aldimines with diborylmethane to form chiral β-aminoboronates, which are valuable synthetic building blocks in organic synthesis. The developed copper-catalytic system was also extended to a copper-catalyzed SN2′-selective allylic substitution reaction using readily accessible allylic chlorides and 1,1-diborylalkanes, a reaction which proceeds with chemoselective C−B bond activation of the 1,1-diborylalkanes. This method provided an useful approach to afford branched alkylboronate esters.

intro.text:
We aim to provide better decision-making strategies for several types of stakeholders based on the better understanding of future dynamics in complex systems and interactions among stakeholders. Our approaches are mainly based on various techniques from optimization, stochastic process, and also economics.

Particularly, we have been conducting researches about “Business Operation/Policy Design” and “Sequential/Multi-agent Decision System Operation” based on (1) Optimization models under uncertainty (stochastic programming, robust optimization),  (2) sequential decision process models (dynamic programming, reinforcement learning), and (3) multi-agent system models (game theory, multi-agent learning).

intro.text:
Research
The research topics, we are particularly interested in, are

• Novel energy materials based on metal-hydrides
• Hydrogen storage materials

• Hydrogen embrittlement

• In-situ characterization of catalyst & hydrogen energy materials
Metal-hydrides are typically formed through the diffusion of hydrogen atoms into metals. Unlike this conventional approach, we have pioneered a new synthetic paradigm that enables material synthesis in a hydrogen rich environment, leading to the discovery of novel metal-hydride materials with unique crystal structures and distinctive properties. We are conducting fundamental research in materials science aims to extend this new synthetic pathway based on radiation chemistry to discover novel metastable metal-hydride materials.

We are further advancing toward scalable synthesis processes, exploring both laser-based and electron accelerator driven approaches as complementary pathways for metastable metal hydride synthesis, and have demonstrated successful laser-based synthesis of metal-hydride materials.

These novel metal-hydrides can provide promising options for applications in solid-state hydrogen storage systems, super-conductors and catalysts.[Nature (2022), AFM (2024)]

Hydrogen Storage Materials
It is essential to develop safe and high-performance hydrogen storage systems to ensure the widespread use of hydrogen energy. Our research focuses on the development of next-generation hydrogen storage materials for solid-state hydrogen storage systems. We synthesize hydrogen storage alloys and systematically investigate their structural, thermodynamic, and kinetic properties during hydrogen uptake and release. In particular, we aim to understand the mechanisms responsible for performance enhancement and degradation, including hydrogenation reactions, phase transformations, defect evolution, and interactions with impurities, across length scales from the nanoscale to the bulk scale. For these studies, we employ advanced characterization techniques, such as in-situ transmission electron microscopy(TEM), in-situ X-ray diffraction(XRD), and four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy(4D-STEM), to directly observe and analyze metal–hydrogen reactions and related structural changes. Through these efforts, we aim to establish design rules for hydrogen energy materials and develop advanced hydrogen storage alloys with fast kinetics, high storage capacity, and strong resistance to various impurities, thereby contributing to the realization of a sustainable hydrogen society.
