Research Topics (ENG)
Our Vision
The Nanotrio refers to a class of diverse nanomaterials developed at the intersection of nanophotonics, nanoplasmonics, and nanobiotechnology. Our research explores the synthesis, characterization, and potential applications of nanomaterials, with a particular focus on quantum dots, plasmonic nanoparticles, and nanocomposites with tunable morphologies and sophisticated nanostructures.
We specialize in characterizing the “small world” of nanomaterials using absorption and emission spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy, dynamic light scattering, and zeta-potential analysis. Through these analyses, we investigate the properties of synthesized materials and use the resulting insights to guide the future design of functional nanomaterials.
Our goal is to understand the unique physical properties of nanomaterials and translate them into practical applications in nanotherapy, nanoenergy, nanodiagnostics, and other emerging fields.
Ongoing Research Projects (For more information, please visit the Project page)
Our Nanotrio laboratory conducts research in nanoscience and nanobiology, focusing on the interaction between light and matter at the nanoscale. We study the synthesis, surface control, assembly, and complexation of nanocrystals to develop nanostructures and advanced materials with potential applications in displays, photodetectors, photovoltaics, photoelectrochemical cells, sensors, and bioimaging. In particular, we study semiconductor nanocrystals, such as quantum dots and QLED materials, as well as nanostructured materials based on gold nanoparticles that can be used for sensing and three-dimensional cell imaging. By leveraging the unique physical properties of nanomaterials, we aim to develop functional materials for a wide range of optical, electronic, and biomedical applications.
We synthesize new nanocrystals by controlling precursor reactivity and reaction intermediates. Quantum dots are inorganic nanocrystals with a molecular-level size distribution, and their small size allows a large number of atoms to reside at the surface. For example, InP quantum dots, which are widely used in QLED displays, can contain approximately 1,000 to 10,000 atoms, depending on the size. Although the exact atomic structure and growth mechanism of these nanocrystals remain difficult to determine, quantized intermediates can form during their synthesis. These intermediates are structurally analogous to the critical nuclei described in classical nucleation theory. Our research focuses on understanding these intermediate nanoclusters and controlling their formation through precursor chemistry, with the goal of establishing growth pathways and mechanistic principles for the development of high-performance QLED nanocrystals.
We also investigate surface chemistry at the nanoscale. Surface chemistry is essential for forming efficient conjugates with proteins, DNA, and antibodies, and it plays a critical role in controlling colloidal stability and surface functionality. In particular, we study ultrafast surface modification using quantized ions and investigate reversible surface bonding based on hydrogen-bonding interactions. Through these approaches, we aim to establish precise and efficient strategies for tailoring nanocrystal surfaces.
Another major focus of our research is near-infrared optical materials. Compared with conventional molecular or organic materials, quantum dots can emit in the near-infrared region while exhibiting high photostability and size-tunable optical properties. Quantum-dot-based optical probes can also be miniaturized and used for ultrahigh-sensitivity sensing through solution-based processes such as inkjet printing. Using these properties, we develop new near-infrared fluorescent probes and materials. In addition, we are developing brain–computer interfaces that use autonomous quantum-dot probes to visualize real-time physiological signals in the brain, thereby enabling new approaches for understanding human cognition and neural activity. We are also synthesizing biocompatible nanocrystals and converting them into oil-in-fluorocarbon materials for biomedical applications.
We develop nanorobotic probes that respond to environmental stimuli, such as pH, by changing their optical properties. Like cuttlefish that change color in response to their surroundings, these nanorobotic probes are designed to alter their optical signals when exposed to specific environments. Quantum-dot optical probes can also be used as next-generation display materials because they provide a wide color gamut and can respond sensitively to external stimuli. By programming their response to specific conditions, these probes can visualize changes that are difficult to detect directly. For example, quantum dots that respond to magnetic field variations are being investigated as magnetoplasmonic nanorobot probes that use gold nanoparticles and can be applied to next-generation transparent displays, including AR and VR technologies.
Finally, we are developing barcode technologies using near-infrared probes to overcome the limitations of conventional molecular probes and to enable simultaneous detection of multiple targets. Because of their strong photostability, high brightness, and narrow emission bandwidth, quantum dots can provide highly multiplexed optical signals. Antibody–quantum dot conjugates can be used for rapid and quantitative target detection in complex biological environments. These nanomaterials offer advantages for medical diagnosis, bioimaging, and precision sensing by minimizing biological background interference and providing distinct multicolor optical signals. Through this research, we aim to develop quantum-dot-based molecular barcode platforms capable of detecting multiple professional-level diagnostic signals simultaneously.

Nanophotonics
The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be precisely controlled, making them versatile materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices. Our group synthesizes a wide range of nanomaterials, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous structures. We have demonstrated the photomodulation of QD conjugates using additional UV excitation, which promotes electron transfer to the QDs and quenches their photoluminescence. We have also developed inorganic-ligand-capped QDs as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
1. Optical properties of quantum dots
Semiconductor nanocrystals, commonly referred to as quantum dots (QDs), differ from bulk semiconductors in that their optical properties are strongly dependent on size. In semiconductor nanocrystals with diameters of only a few nanometers, electrons and holes are confined within a space smaller than the exciton Bohr radius, giving rise to quantum confinement in all three dimensions. This confinement produces discrete electronic energy levels and makes the band gap (BG) between the valence band and the conduction band dependent on nanocrystal size. The BG determines the energy required for photoexcitation and the subsequent radiative relaxation process. As the size of a QD decreases, the BG increases, leading to absorption and fluorescence at shorter wavelengths (Fig. 1). QD core/shell structure can be classified into type-I and type-II (Fig. 2)
Semiconductor QDs can be categorized into type-I and type-II structures according to their band alignment. In type-I QDs, the shell material has a larger BG than the core material, allowing the electron–hole pair to be confined within the core. This confinement enhances photoluminescence (PL) efficiency, making type-I QDs useful for highly emissive applications. In type-II QDs, the valence and conduction band edges of the core and shell are staggered, which spatially separates electrons and holes across the core/shell interface (Fig. 3a). This charge separation makes type-II QDs attractive for energy-conversion applications, including solar cells. Changes in the valence and conduction band alignment of the core and shell alter the spatial distribution of electron and hole densities. This band engineering also creates an effective BG that is not determined solely by the intrinsic band gaps of the constituent materials, enabling control over both absorption and PL wavelengths (Fig. 3).
Colloidal nanocrystals synthesized from solution-phase precursors offer broad tunability in morphology and size, providing many opportunities for functional applications. Morphological control is important because nanocrystal shape and internal structure influence electronic energy states, charge-carrier mobility, and exciton localization. These morphologies can be controlled by regulating nucleation and growth processes from the atomic level. Such processes are governed by both kinetic factors, including reactant concentration and diffusion, and thermodynamic factors, including surfactant concentration and reaction temperature. Solution-based synthesis can produce highly crystalline nanocrystals with diverse shapes and offers notable advantages over conventional top-down methods. We synthesize various types of nanocrystals, including core/shell QDs, nanorods, nanotetrapods, and nanoporous materials (Fig. 4a). We have also reported supra-QDs (SQDs) (Fig. 4b), which are hierarchical superstructures composed of hundreds of individual QDs, each only a few nanometers in size, assembled through oriented attachment. These SQDs may exhibit enhanced charge-carrier mobility and therefore show strong potential as sensitizers for solar-cell applications.
2. Investigation of the properties of NPs induced by the incorporation of foreign atoms
Introducing foreign atoms into as-synthesized nanocrystals can alter their optical, electrical, and magnetic properties in addition to changing their composition. Depending on the amount and distribution of the introduced species, this process can be classified in several ways. One representative approach is doping, in which semiconductor nanocrystals are modified in a manner analogous to the doping of bulk semiconductors.
Doping is the intentional incorporation of foreign atoms into a pristine semiconductor host material to modulate its optical, electrical, and magnetic properties. In bulk semiconductors, dopants ionize and provide additional electrons or holes depending on their valence states. In the case of transition-metal dopants, the dopant spin can couple with the orbitals of the host material. Because of these characteristics, doped semiconductors are widely used in semiconductor junction structures, including transistors and diodes.
In semiconductor nanocrystals, however, doping is strongly affected by quantum confinement and therefore produces behaviors distinct from those observed in bulk materials. The confinement of excitons within an extremely small volume enhances their interaction with dopant ions, amplifying changes in optoelectronic and magnetic properties. Doped nanocrystals therefore have potential applications in memory devices, photocatalysts, and bioimaging probes, in addition to conventional semiconductor junction structures.
Cation exchange is another method for introducing foreign atoms into a crystal lattice. Because bonding in many semiconductor nanocrystals has substantial ionic character, newly introduced cations can replace original cations while preserving the anion framework. This transformation enables the synthesis of sophisticated nanostructures, including metastable crystal phases and complex morphologies that are difficult to access through direct synthesis.
By controlling the amount of foreign ions, cation exchange can be used for doping, heterostructure formation, or the synthesis of entirely new materials. The exchange reaction is driven by differences in the thermodynamic stability of the reactants and products, as well as by ligand-mediated complexation under specific reaction conditions. The feasibility of a given exchange reaction can be evaluated by considering the reaction conditions, solubility products, and standard enthalpies of formation of the relevant materials (Fig 5).
In nanocrystals, even when the constituent materials are identical, the crystal structures obtained after cation exchange can differ depending on particle size because thermodynamic stability is size-dependent (Fig. 6). Therefore, investigating how cation-exchange outcomes vary with nanocrystal size is important for understanding the reaction mechanism. After cation exchange, optical spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, and other atomic-level characterization methods should be used to confirm the composition and crystal structure of the final material.
3. PL modulation of QD
The emission wavelength and intensity of QDs can be modulated, making them promising materials for switchable probes in cellular and whole-body imaging, optical modulation, and light-emitting devices. We used quasi type-II QDs to develop photoluminescence-modulating probes that respond to external stimuli. Charging quasi type-II QDs, in which electrons and holes are spatially separated, induces photoluminescence (PL) spectral switching. The initial emission state can be recovered through a subsequent neutralization step. Reversible PL switching over many repeated cycles was demonstrated by alternating UV excitation between on and off states (Fig. 7). We also developed a modulation sensor based on a PL on/off system. In addition, reversible and wavelength-selective PL modulation was investigated by controlling charge transfer between QDs and quenchers.
4. QD-based Solar Cells
A solar cell (SC) converts light energy directly into electrical energy. Although silicon SCs have been commercialized on a large scale, they remain costly and require complex fabrication processes. Nanocrystal-based SCs offer a potentially simpler and more cost-effective alternative. Several types of SCs use QDs, including QD-sensitized SCs, hybrid SCs composed of QDs and conducting polymers (Fig. 8), and Schottky-type SCs.
Although these SCs have different device architectures, they all rely on light absorption followed by charge generation, separation, and transport. Charge separation and transfer are influenced by the morphology of the QDs and the structure of the active layer. The use of QDs allows the absorption wavelength to be tuned, and their colloidal dispersibility in various solvents enables solution-processable device fabrication. Therefore, QD-based SCs represent a promising research direction for developing low-cost solar-energy conversion technologies. By identifying the conditions required for high power conversion efficiency, experimental studies can provide insights into simple and scalable fabrication strategies for QD-based SCs.

Nanoplasmonics
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) arises when free electrons in metal nanoparticles collectively oscillate in resonance with incident electromagnetic energy at the interface between the metal and the surrounding dielectric medium. Noble metal nanoparticles exhibit strong SPR when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale, and their optical properties can be precisely tuned by controlling the metal composition, particle size and shape, and local dielectric environment. These tunable SPR characteristics make noble metal nanoparticles highly versatile platforms for spectroscopic analysis, optical imaging, sensing, and therapeutic applications. Our group develops advanced metal nanoparticle complexes for highly efficient cancer therapy and photoacoustic-guided drug delivery.
Properties of Surface Plasmon Resonance
Conductive metals contain a high density of free electrons that are not strongly localized to individual atoms. Because these electrons can collectively respond to external electromagnetic fields, metallic nanostructures can exhibit surface plasmon resonance (SPR) when their dimensions are reduced to the nanoscale. SPR gives metal nanoparticles unique optical properties. In particular, noble metal nanoparticles, such as gold and silver nanoparticles, interact strongly with visible light and exhibit intense absorption and scattering, with optical cross sections that are orders of magnitude larger than those of typical organic dyes. They also show high resistance to oxidation and photobleaching, making them powerful optical probes that can complement or replace conventional organic fluorophores.
The optical responses of noble metal nanoparticles are highly tunable because their plasmon resonance can be controlled by the dielectric properties of the metal, as well as by the size, shape, and local environment of the nanostructure. Our goal is to design and synthesize diverse metallic nanostructures and to investigate their optical properties using spectroscopic and imaging tools. We further aim to apply these nanostructures to biological and biomedical systems (Fig. 1).
Study of Thermotherapy for Tumor Cells
Photothermal therapy is a cancer treatment strategy in which absorbed photon energy is converted into heat to induce cancer cell death (Fig. 2). Because cancer cells are generally more sensitive to elevated temperatures than normal cells, selective heat generation within tumor tissues can improve therapeutic efficacy while reducing damage to surrounding healthy tissue. Metal nanoparticles are highly effective photothermal agents because of their strong light absorption and efficient photothermal conversion. By controlling the thermal energy generated through the photothermal effect of metal nanoparticles, selective cancer therapy can be achieved.
Near-infrared (NIR) light is widely used for photothermal therapy because it penetrates deeply into living tissues and is only weakly absorbed or scattered by major biomolecules such as hemoglobin and water. The therapeutic selectivity of pH-responsive “smart” gold nanoparticles that absorb NIR light preferentially in cancer cells or tumor tissues can be further enhanced by exploiting the acidic and hypoxic microenvironment of tumors. In addition, nanoparticle-mediated photothermal treatment can be combined with anticancer drugs to achieve synergistic therapeutic effects. Gold nanoparticle aggregation can be induced through various strategies. For example, DNA hydrogel–nanoparticle complexes can be designed to release anticancer drugs while simultaneously promoting nanoparticle aggregation, providing a platform for combined photothermal and chemotherapeutic treatment (Fig 3).
Dark-Field Microscopy
Dark-field microscopy (DFM) visualizes scattered light from a specimen, whereas conventional transmission-mode microscopy forms images using transmitted light. Metal nanoparticles can generate strong contrast under DFM because they efficiently scatter incident light at wavelengths that match their SPR. Because scattering signals from small metal nanoparticles are intense and highly sensitive to plasmonic properties, DFM enables optical visualization even at the single-particle level.
DFM is also useful for distinguishing materials that may show only weak contrast in conventional imaging modes. This capability allows the SPR properties of individual metal nanoparticles to be characterized and enables biological imaging using metal nanoparticles as scattering-based contrast agents (Fig. 4).
Photoacoustic Imaging Using “Smart” Gold Nanoparticles
Photoacoustic imaging (PAI) is an emerging hybrid imaging modality that combines optical excitation with ultrasound detection. As a nonionizing biomedical imaging method, PAI can provide molecular and functional information, including hemoglobin oxygen saturation, blood flow, and tissue morphology. It is therefore well suited for biomedical studies, including the monitoring of tumor physiology and treatment responses.
In PAI, image contrast is determined by the optical absorption properties of the target. Exogenous contrast agents with strong near-infrared (NIR) absorption can enhance PA signals because NIR light penetrates deeply into biological tissues. “Smart” gold nanoparticles (SANs) can rapidly aggregate under mildly acidic conditions, which are commonly found in tumor microenvironments. This aggregation induces a red shift in their absorption spectrum toward the red and NIR regions. As a result, PA amplitude increases under mildly acidic conditions while remaining relatively unchanged at physiological pH. By combining tumor accumulation with high PA conversion efficiency, SANs can significantly amplify PA signals in cell-level and small-animal experiments (Fig. 6). These properties make SANs a promising platform for PA-guided drug delivery, enabling real-time identification of delivery targets and on-demand therapeutic administration.

Nanobiotechnology
QD-based optical probes provide a promising platform for in vivo bioimaging and next-generation medical imaging applications because of their bright luminescence, resistance to photobleaching, and size-tunable emission wavelengths. Our group develops NIR-II-emitting QD probes and has demonstrated cancer diagnosis using QD–antibody conjugates. We have also engineered amphiphilic polyethylenimine-derivative platforms that incorporate QDs for cell labeling, targeted delivery, gene delivery, and ratiometric oxygen sensing.
1. Biological applications of Quantum dots
Semiconductor QDs present a possible new technology for in vivo bio-imaging and future medical-imaging applications. QDs have proven potential as imaging contrast agents due to their bright luminescence, their resistance to photobleaching, and their tunable emission wavelengths. The main impediment to the use of QDs for biological applications is their biocompatibility. QDs that contain toxic elements such as Cd, Pb, Hg, or As have limited biological applications. High quality ‘non-toxic’ QDs have been synthesized (e.g., InP, ZnTe/ZnSe, CuInS2; AgInS2); they are free from potential leakage of toxic heavy-metal ions, and photoluminesce at wavelengths that can be selected by adjusting the size of the QD. The new methods of synthesizing ‘non-toxic’ QDs using various solvents and QD precursors have been investigated to obtain bright and photostable QDs that promise application to in vivo medical imaging.
2. Surface modification, functionalization and bioconjugation of QDs for biological applications
QDs are synthesized in inorganic solvent to obtain high quality, so their surfaces should be modified for bioimaging applications. The surface molecules for QDs should give good colloidal stabilities in aqueous solutions without aggregation, and should have appropriate sites to allow conjugation with biomolecules. To be suitable for applications in targeted imaging or in long-term in vivo imaging, QDs must be colloidally stable and must have minimal non-specific binding. QDs that have been modified to have zwitterionic surface molecules can maintain colloidal stability over broad ranges of pH and ionic strength, and to show minimal non-specific adsorptions (Fig. 1). Moreover, the zwitterionic QD surface ligands can also be used in conjunction with other functional groups; this trait allows simple conjugations for highly specific targeting while retaining the advantages of a zwitterionic QD surface (Fig. 2).
3. Cancer Diagnosis Using QD - Antibody Conjugates
Cancer is a very heterogeneous system. Multiplexed QD imaging is well-suited to detecting such heterogeneous systems. QDs are also bright, photostable, and allow multiplexing by a single excitation wavelength. QDs have broad absorption profile with large one-photon and two-photon absorption cross sections, narrow and symmetric emission profile, and large effective Stokes shifts. To improve the accuracy of cancer detection, multiple biological targets must be imaged concurrently; these advantages of QDs can be used in multiplexing to achieve fluorescence molecular imaging of cancer tissues. Doctors frequently use endoscopy to detect colon cancer, but the diagnosis is based on the clinician's naked-eye perception, which is subjective and error-prone.We developed a rapid and accurate molecular fluorescence imaging technique that uses antibody (Ab)-coated QDs (Ab-QDs) that are sprayed and washed simultaneously on colon tumor tissues inside live animals, then excited and imaged by endoscopy. QDs were conjugated to matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9, MMP 14, or carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) Abs with zwitterionic surface coating to reduce nonspecific bindings. The Ab-QD probes can diagnose tumors on sectioned mouse tissues, in fresh mouse colons stained ex vivo and in vivo, and in fresh human colon adenoma tissues in 30 min and can be imaged to a depth of 100 μm. The probes successfully detected not only cancers that are readily discernible to the naked eye, but also hyperplasia and adenoma regions. Sum and cross-signal operations provided post-processed images that can show complementary information or regions of high priority (Fig. 3). This multiplexed QD, spray-and-wash, and endoscopy approach provides a significant advantage for detecting small or flat tumors that may be missed by conventional endoscopic examinations and bestows a strategy for the improvement of cancer diagnosis.
4. NIR-II emitting QD probes
The NIR biological window from 650 nm to 1700 nm allows deeper penetration than visible light into biological tissues such as skin and blood, because these tissues scatter and absorb less light at long wavelengths than at short wavelengths. The window between 650 nm and 950 nm (NIR-I) has been exploited extensively for in vivo optical imaging of live animals, but little research has considered use of the longer-wavelength window (NIR-II) from 1000 to 1700 nm for in vivo fluorescence imaging of live animals. Light scattering and absorption by biomolecules are much weaker in the NIR-II region than in NIR-I, so tissue penetration depth and spatial resolution are increased, and autofluorescence is decreased in NIR-II. QDs can be advantageous fluorescent probes for molecular imaging in both the NIR-I and the NIR-II region. CdTeSe, and CuInS2 have been developed as fluorophores in NIR-I, and have shown high photostability and quantum yield (QY) > 50%. PbS and Ag2S QDs have been developed for NIR-II fluorescence imaging applications, and showed QY > 10% with inorganic shells in the aqueous phase (Fig. 4). We report an enzyme-activatable NIR-II probe that exhibits fluorescence (FL) upon matrix metalloprotease activity in tumor microenvironment. Bright and stable PbS/CdS/ZnS core/shell/shell QDs were synthesized as a model NIR-II fluorophore, and activatable modulators were attached to exploit photoexcited electron transfer (PET) quenching. The quasi-type-II QD band alignment allowed rapid and effective FL modulations with a compact surface ligand modulator that contains methylene blue PET quencher. The modulator was optimized to afford full enzyme accessibility and high activation signal surge when the enzyme was active. In a colon-cancer mouse model, the probe demonstrated selective FL activation at tumor sites with tripled signal strength in 10 min (Fig. 5).

The modulator was optimized to afford full enzyme accessibility and high activation signal surge when the enzyme was active. 5. Sensing molecule by using QDs
Amphiphilic polyethyleneimine derivatives (amPEIs) were synthesized and used to encapsulate dozens of QDs. The QD-amPEI composite was ~100 nm in hydrodynamic diameter and had an outer surface with a slight positive charge that is well suited for cellular internalization. The outer positive surface was further exploited for gene delivery and targeting. Co-delivery of QDs and GFP-silencing RNAs was demonstrated by attaching siRNAs to the outer surface; the process achieved transfection efficiency that was an order of magnitude higher than conventional gene transfections. Hyaluronic acids were tethered onto the QD-amPEI for cell-specific targeted labeling, which achieved a specific-to-nonspecific signal ratio > 100. The inside hydrophobic compartment was further applied to cohost oxygen-sensing phosphorescence Ru dyes along with QDs. The ratiometric PL signals of the QD-Ru-amPEI oxygen probe show accurate and reversible oxygen-sensing capability and were successfully applied to cellular and spheroid models (Fig. 6).

I am an assistant professor in Graduate School of AI and Computer Science & Engineering at POSTECH. Before joining POSTECH, I was an associate professor in AI Graduate School at GIST and a Researcher at the Intelligent Convergence Research Laboratory, ETRI. I had been a postdoctoral researcher in the Computer Vision Lab. at the Seoul National University. I received my Ph.D. degree from POSTECH, under the supervision of Prof. Bohyung Han and Minsu Cho, and B.S. and M.S degrees from the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Ewha Womans University.
My research interests lie in the intersection of computer vision, machine learning and deep learning, which include visual tracking, object detection, segmentation, and learning with minimal or no supervision by human. I am also particularly interested in trustworthy and robust AI, with a focus on combating deepfakes, protecting visual data from malicious manipulation, and building reliable vision systems that can be safely deployed in real-world environments.

본문 바로가기
Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding
Open-vocabulary scene understanding reflects a paradigm shift away from recognition systems built around a small, fixed set of predefined categories. Classical segmentation and detection models can only recognize the specific classes they were trained on — a "chair" model has no way to name or localize a "stool" if that word was never in its label set. Open-vocabulary perception instead couples visual recognition with language, letting a model segment, ground, and reason about an arbitrary object category described in natural language at test time, whether or not that category ever appeared in training.
Active Perception
Active perception is grounded in a paradigm shift that computer vision underwent as it moved beyond passive, all-at-once scene analysis. Rather than treating a camera or a model as a fixed device that must take in an entire scene and try to make sense of everything it sees, active perception treats the observer as something that can choose — where to look, how to move through and interact with a scene, or which view to prioritize — in order to answer a specific question as efficiently as possible.
Embodied AI & Language-Driven Robot Manipulation
The lab's embodied AI line investigates why end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle with long-horizon manipulation, and proposes a modular approach centered on open-vocabulary affordance grounding rather than mapping instructions directly to low-level actions. The core hypothesis is that manipulation becomes tractable when it is decomposed into intermediate, physically grounded representations — where on an object a task-relevant region is, how a hand should contact it, and how the whole body should move to get there — rather than learned as one opaque instruction-to-action mapping. This is a deliberate move away from black-box, end-to-end learning toward a more analytical and explicit formulation of manipulation, where each intermediate representation can be inspected, interpreted, and reasoned about on its own terms.
Scene Graphs & Human-Centric Scene Parsing
Understanding a visual scene often requires more than naming the objects in it — it requires parsing the scene into a structured representation of entities and the relationships between them. A scene graph makes this explicit: nodes for objects, edges for their relationships, turning an image into a graph rather than a flat list of detections. When the entities being related are people — interacting with objects, forming groups, or simply needing to be perceived accurately in the first place — this general scene-parsing problem becomes human-centric, and the lab's work in this space treats human-object interaction, group and social behavior, and even pose perception as specialized instances of the same underlying graph-parsing challenge.
Symmetry Analysis & Equivariant Learning
Many visual patterns aren't arbitrary — they're structured by symmetry: an object looks the same after a reflection, a rotation, or some other transformation. Building models that can detect this structure, or that inherently respect it, is a distinct research problem from ordinary recognition, because standard convolutional and attention architectures have no built-in notion of "this feature should transform predictably when the input does." The lab has a sustained line of work addressing this gap from two complementary angles: finding where symmetry exists in an image or shape, and building network architectures that are structurally equivariant to transformations like rotation and reflection by design.
Actions, Events & Long-Horizon Reasoning from Videos
Beyond recognizing what is in a single frame, video understanding requires reasoning about how content unfolds over time — segmenting a stream into meaningful units, anticipating what comes next, locating precise moments of change, answering questions that require following a narrative, and tracking specific objects reliably as they move and occlude. The lab has a sustained program across all of these temporal reasoning problems, and a defining trend across the group's recent work is treating generative modeling — diffusion in particular — and large language models not as end tasks in themselves, but as flexible backbones for representing and reasoning about temporal structure.
Relational Representation Learning for Video Understanding
Before a system can reason about actions, events, or long video narratives, it first needs a way to represent motion itself — and for a long stretch of the lab's history, that representation problem was treated as unsolved rather than assumed. Standard video architectures apply spatio-temporal convolution or attention uniformly across space and time, treating motion as something that emerges implicitly from stacked appearance features. This line of the lab's research instead argues that motion has its own structure — correspondence and relation between neighboring regions across time — and that structure should be modeled explicitly rather than left to convolution or attention to discover on its own.
Visual Correspondence & Geometric Matching
Finding reliable correspondences between images, shapes, and point clouds is one of the lab's longest-running research threads, tracing back over a decade to early work on semantic correspondence with object proposals and continuing through today's group-equivariant formulations. The core problem is deceptively simple to state — given two visual observations of related content, which parts correspond to which? — but solving it robustly across viewpoint change, intra-class variation, symmetry, and partial observability has proven to be a deep and recurring research challenge.

Curriculum Vitae
I am an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering and the Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence at POSTECH.
I lead the Health and Human-Computer Interaction (H2CI) Lab.
As a human-computer interaction (HCI), computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), and Health researcher, I examine how health monitoring technology can better account for infrastructural complexity of clinical and public health care. My research approach encompasses understanding how stakeholders use existing health monitoring tools through interviews, surveys, and log analysis; developing prototypes to explore novel design ideas; and evaluating these designs through real-world field deployments.
My work has been recognized with 2026 ACM SIGCHI Outstanding Dissertation Award, a Best Paper Award at CHI 2023, and the Google PhD Fellowship (2023-2025). My research has also been featured in the LA Times, Kaiser Family Foundation Health News, and Digital Chosun.
I received my PhD in Informatics at the University of California, Irvine (Advised by Daniel A. Epstein). I completed MS in Computer Graphics Technology (Advised by Austin Toombs) at Purdue University, BA in Information Science & Culture, and BA in Consumer and Child Studies at Seoul National University.
I have worked as a research intern with Young-Ho Kim at NAVER AI Lab and as a researcher at the National Center for Mental Health in South Korea with Hwajung Hong.

intro.text:
Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD)
We focuses on developing advanced deep learning-based fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) systems for complex industrial equipment.
We aim to solve key challenges encountered in real-world settings, such as the scarcity of fault data and distribution shifts between training and operational environments.

Research Topic
Handling Data Scarcity
We develop algorithms that can detect both known and unknown fault types, even with very few faulty samples, by integrating open-set recognition (OSR).

Research Topic
Ensuring Robustness
We research domain generalization techniques to ensure our FDD models remain reliable and accurate even when operating conditions change.

Research Topic
Analyzing Complex Sensor Data
We apply deep learning to analyze multivariate time-series data from various sensors to capture subtle signs of failure early.

UWB Application
Head Orientation Tracking
Head orientation tracking determines which way a user's head is facing. For more accurate and energy-efficient performance on edge devices, we utilizes Ultra-Wideband (UWB) technology with an extended Kalman filter for calibration. This approach enables precise orientation tracking using solely UWB measurements.

Acoustic Sensing
Aim to make everyday mobile devices be accurate, accessible for natural interaction and context sensing.
Mobile systems that emits and analyzes sound waves by on-board speaker and microphone.
Learning-based inference and real-time prototyping to achieve robust, power-efficient system.
Voice AI

Research Topic
Emotional Voice Conversion
Emotional Voice Conversion is the process of transforming an utterance into a different emotion. Recently, research has focused on combining deep learning and representation learning to achieve more natural and subtle emotional expressions, expanding toward modeling temporal emotion variations, generating mixed emotions, and controlling prosody and intonation based on emotions.

Research Topic
Spoken Dialogue System
A Spoken Dialogue System is an AI system that enables natural human-computer interaction through speech by integrating Automatic Speech Recognition(ASR), natural language understanding, and spoken response generation. Recent advances combine LLMs with speech deep learning to enhance contextual reasoning, emotional adaptability, and real-time conversational fluency.

Our research interests are 1) drought mechanisms, risk, and predictability, 2) large-scale land surface modeling focusing on the land cover and use change impact, 3) river and reservoir monitoring via remote senesing and unmanned vehicles, and 4) socio-hydrology with a focus on the dynamics of social response during water-related disasters.

Group Motto:
"We are committed to maintaining integrity in our scholarly products, ownership of our intellectual properties, citizenship of our group, and diversity in our community. "
We strive to increase society's resilience to natural disasters through an integrative understanding of social-natural systems. The natural hazards we study include drought, heatwave, wildfire, flood, earthquake, and compound extremes. Our analyses span various spatiotemporal scales, ranging from catchment- to global-level and sub-seasonal to decadal timescales. Our approach is interdisciplinary converging hydrology, climatology, hydraulics, and social psychology. We hope this will advance our understanding of the coupled dynamics between social and natural systems.
We always keep an eye out for new research collaboration opportunities. If you are interested in our past or current projects, please feel free to contact us.

Big data have hidden, but meaningful, information about our society's behavior and response to influential events. For example, water-related disasters, such as drought and flood, cause rapid increase in public awareness/interest when they happen. Despite the skillful prediction, lack of timely social response to these disaster exacerbates their adverse effects including fatalities and economic losses.
To transform our society to a water-related disaster-ready environment, better understanding of social dynamics (potential triggers and growth and decay patterns of public interest/awareness) is warranted. Lately, big data from information search activities in the cyberspace provide high-resolution records with the unprecedented sample size.
Our research group aims to advance the current knowledge of not only the current prediction skill but also the social response during the emergency of natural/human disasters related to water resources. intro.text:
Semiconductor Materials and
Devices Laboratory
Pohang University of Science and Technology
Topic 01
Metal halide perovskite semiconductors have demonstrated outstanding performance in optoelectronic devices such as solar cells, LEDs, and transistors, thanks to their excellent properties and ease of processing. In particular, they offer new possibilities for implementing CMOS circuits through low-cost, low-temperature processes, addressing the growing demand for high-mobility p-type semiconductors.
View More
Topic 02
P-type Metal Oxide Semiconductors
P-type metal oxide semiconductors have emerged as materials of significant interest in the low-power electronics industry due to their good stability and low off-state current. Their potential applications span a wide array of technologies, including transistors, transparent electronics, display systems, and photovoltaic devices. However, in contrast to the superior electrical performance of n-type metal oxides, the involvement of the oxygen 2p orbital in p-type counterparts leads to localization of the valence band maximum (VBM). This electronic characteristic results in reduced hole mobility within p-type semiconductors. Our research is dedicated to enhancing hole mobility and optimizing the on/off current ratio in p-type materials to overcome these limitations.
View More
Topic 03
Two-Dimensional Layered Semiconductors
2D semiconductors exhibit unique characteristics that make them highly promising for next-generation electronic devices. With atomically thin layers, they enable excellent gate control even at ultra-short channel lengths, supporting continued transistor miniaturization. Their dangling-bond-free surfaces minimize interface trap states, allowing for high carrier mobility and low contact resistance, essential for improved device performance. Additionally, 2D semiconductors offer tunable electronic properties, such as adjustable bandgaps depending on layer thickness. Our research focuses on their potential for integration into flexible electronics, low-power devices, and 3D monolithic structures, highlight 2D semiconductors as a transformative material for future semiconductor technology.
View More

Semiconductor Materials and Devices Lab
Our Mission
Our Mission 목록
Our group pioneers cutting-edge research in advanced semiconductors, focusing on metal halide perovskites, p-type metal oxide semiconductors, and 2D van der Waals materials to revolutionize next-generation optoelectronic devices. By unraveling key properties and optimizing material design, we aim to develop high-performance, cost-effective solutions for applications like thin-film transistors and CMOS circuits. Our mission is to drive innovation in sustainable electronics through interdisciplinary exploration and technological breakthroughs.
Metal Halide Perovskite
Semiconductors
P-type Metal Oxide
Semiconductors
Two-Dimensional Layered
Semiconductors
The past two decades have witnessed the enormous success of metal halide perovskite semiconductors in various optoelectronic devices, like solar cells, LEDs, and most recently transistors, due to an ideal set of optoelectronic properties and processing capability. In particular, considering the urgent demand for high-mobility p-type semiconductors, metal halide perovskite provides a new opportunity to create CMOS circuits in a low-temperature and cost-effective way. Despite certain performance improvements that have been achieved through material design, film processing, and device engineering, a critical understanding of the key properties and potential of these emerging materials for transistor application remains lacking. Therefore, we intend to develop halide perovskite semiconductors for high performance p-type thin-film transistors for commercialization. This project mainly studies the topics below but not limited to this.
TOP

Fuel Cell
A fuel cell uses the chemical energy of hydrogen or another fuel to cleanly and efficiently produce electricity. If hydrogen is the fuel, electricity, water, and heat are the only products. Fuel cells are unique in terms of the variety of their potential applications; they can provide power for systems as large as a utility power station and as small as a laptop computer. Fuel cells can operate at higher efficiencies than combustion engines, and can convert the chemical energy in the fuel to electrical energy with efficiencies of up to 60%. Fuel cells have lower emissions than combustion engines. Hydrogen fuel cells emit only water, so there are no carbon dioxide emissions and no air pollutants that create smog and cause health problems at the point of operation. Also, fuel cells are quiet during operation as they have fewer moving parts.

Battery
Recent development of Electrical vehicles, and portable devices requires high capacity and energy density batteries. Many other researches were conducted to develop electrical performance of the batteries. Such as doping, electrode surface modification and etc. However closer research in atomic and electronic scale research was barely accomplished. Our group closely investigate the structural or electrical phenomenon, utilizing PLS(Pohang Light Source). We expect this research will provide fundamental understanding of battery performance in atomic scale and further development of high capacity and energy density energy.

Water Electrolysis
Water electrolysis(also called water splitting) is the decomposition of water into oxygen and hydrogen gas due to the passage of an electric current. This technique can be used to make hydrogen gas, a main component of hydrogen fuel, and breathable oxygen gas. It ideally requires a potential difference of 1.23 V to split water. However, real water electrolyzers require higher voltages for the reaction to proceed. The part that exceeds 1.23 V is called overpotential, and represents any kind of loss and nonideality in the electrochemical process. Electrocatalysts can facilitate this reaction.

CO2 Reduction
Carbon dioxide is an abundant potential carbon resource on Earth, and it is also a greenhouse gas whose atmospheric concentration has increased sharply over the past two centuries Chemical fixation of carbon dioxide (CO2) is an attractive technique for utilization of carbon resources, as well as for the reduction of the atmospheric concentration of CO2. Carbon dioxide is a potential carbon resource abundant on earth. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 is the conversion of carbon dioxide to more reduced chemical species. The first examples of electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide are from the 19th century, when carbon dioxide was reduced to carbon monoxide using a zinc cathode. Research in this field intensified in the 1980s following the oil embargoes of the 1970s. CO2 can be removed by the reduction that produces various chemicals, such as carbon monoxide (CO), methanol (CH3OH), methane (CH4), and formic acid (HCOOH). In our lab, we are mainly focused on the CO2 reduction to CO using various metallic catalysts.

Anti-corrosion
In modern times, with the development of stainless steel, the corrosion resistance of steel has improved dramatically. However, corrosion in extreme conditions such as cryogenic, high temperatures, abrasion and seawater environments still causes economical loss and environmental damage and has become a major cause of safety issues. Since it is almost impossible to replace and repair corrosion parts in such a harsh environment, the need for structural materials with strong corrosion resistance is increasing day by day. Our group is exploring ways to improve the anti-corrosion properties of structural materials without losing mechanical properties via alloy composition control or surface treatment.

Battery Recycling
In order to meet global target of carbon emission, automotive industries are radically changing. Millions of electric vehicles are now on roads, consequently, tones of end-of-life batteries will come out after decades. In comparison to the number of end-of-life batteries and market size of battery recycling industries in the near future, the development of technology is still lag behind and the players in this field are not enough. Thus, our group set our sight on developing advanced battery recycling technology using hydrometallurgical processes. Battery recycling technology definitely will occupy highly demanding part in battery industries.

Our research goal is to develop a systematic evaluation and design framework for renewable energy technologies by integrating process simulation with life cycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA). Research Topic 5 : Data Prediction with Artificial Intelligence and Mathematical Modeling
Research Goal (연구 목표): 인공지능 및 수학적 모델링 기반 데이터 예측 기법을 통한 공정·소재·에너지 시스템 성능의 정량적 예측
We aim to develop data-driven prediction frameworks by integrating artificial intelligence with mathematical modeling to enhance process and system-level decision-making. Our research focuses on building data platforms for materials and process design, as well as developing machine-learning models for property prediction based on molecular representations. In particular, we target applications such as intelligent semiconductor device design and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) property prediction, enabling standards compliance assessment and optimal pathway through AI-assisted analysis.
▪ 지능형 연구 설계 기반의 3차원 고집적 산화물계 반도체 소자 구현 및 소재-공정 전주기 데이터 HUB 구축 (한국연구재단 나노·소재기술개발사업, ‘25.07.~’29.12.)

Research Topic 6: New Energy Technologies with Process Optimization and Dynamic Modeling
Research Goal (연구 목표): 차세대 에너지 기술 대상 공정 최적화와 정적·동적 모사를 결합한 시스템 수준 분석
We aim to develop system-level modeling and optimization frameworks for new energy technologies by integrating process design, dynamic modeling, and advanced optimization techniques. Our research focuses on catalytic and CCU-based chemical production processes, integrated LNG–SOFC–CCUS systems, and fusion energy fuel cycle technologies, including detritiation systems. Through steady-state and dynamic simulation, as well as data-driven surrogate modeling, we seek to enhance process efficiency, controllability, and environmental performance of emerging energy systems.

intro.text:
MDSB Lab
Molecular Diagnosis and Synthetic Biology
Welcome to the website of molecular diagnosis and synthetic biology lab (http://mdsb.postech.ac.kr) We do research in the field of 1) metabolic engineering and 2) synthetic biology developing useful molecular engineering tools and microorganisms capable of producing various products such as biofuels, commodity chemicals, value-added products, etc. We are located at Environmental Engineering Building (Professor:#325; Students:#310; Lab:#305) and Jigok Research Building (Students:#306; Lab:#301) at POSTECH, Pohang, Korea Lab Openings : We have positions available for enthusiastic graduate students and talented postdocs (Department of Chemical Engineering, Division of Interdisciplinary Bioscience and Bioengineering). Please contact to gyjung@postech.ac.kr Nelson, David L., and Michael M. Cox. Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry. 7th ed., W.H. Freeman, 2017.
Environmental Engineering Building (Professor:#325; Students:#310; Lab:#305) and Jigok Research Building (Students:#306; Lab:#301) at POSTECH, Pohang, Korea
Tel : 054-279-8335
gyjung@postech.ac.kr

LAB introduction
1. Metabolic engineering
In metabolic engineering, enhanced production of value-added chemicals requires precise flux control between growth-essential competing and production pathways, and optimized precursor balance. By engineering genetically tractable strains using these metabolic engineering strategies, efficient conversion of biomass into bioactive compounds, biofuels, and bioplastics can be achieved.
-Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli has been widely regarded as a genetically tractable strain due to its well-characterized genetics, the availability of a wide range of molecular tools, and its high transformation efficiency.
-Vibrio sp.dhg
Brown macroalgae are emerging as a sustainable alternative feedstock with the potential to alleviate concerns about competition for food resources and the limitations of conventional agricultural cultivation. However, about 50% of the carbon components of brown macroalgae are composed of alginate. Most conventional microorganisms cannot metabolize alginate without additional pretreatment, limiting its use as a feedstock. In MDSB lab, we isolated and characterized a fast-growing, alginate-utilizing microorganism, named Vibrio sp. dhg. In contrast to Vibrio natriegens, this strain is capable of robust growth with alginate as the sole carbon source. It has emerged as a promising platform for the efficient conversion of brown macroalgae sugars into diverse value-added biochemicals.
Lim et al., Nat. Commun, 2019
-Bacillus,Pseudomonas, and etc.
They are also being engineered, and other novel strains are being identified.
2. Synthetic Biology
Synthetic biology is a emerging research field to redesign and construct the biological parts, devices, and systems for useful and practical purpose.
We are currently developing new molecular tools, and applying these cutting-edge technologies to design and construct high performance microorganism (mainly Escherichia coli, and Vibrio sp.dhg) for the production of biofuels, commodity chemicals, and bioactive compounds including pharmaceutical proteins from renewable biomass.
1) Fine-tunable and predictable expression level control system
- UTR Designer
: It is a computational tool that predicts and designs the mRNA translation initiation region to modulate translation efficiency in prokaryotes.
↑
Click!
Seo SW, Yang JS et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2013
- Repressor library
The repressor library can be constructed by varying the expression levels of the repressor, based on degenerate 5′ UTR sequence variants generated by UTR Library Designer. Modular application of the repressor library enables fine regulation of the flux between the target product biosynthetic pathway and growth-related pathway, thereby enhancing the production of a diverse range of target chemicals.
JY Lee, S Cha, et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2021
2) Enzyme activity engineering based on sequence co-evolution analysis
- sequence co-evolutionary analysis to control the efficiency of enzyme reactions (SCANEER)
: It uses A.A. sequence information as input to find activity-enhancing mutations in distal site from the active site of the enzyme based on sequence co-evolution analysis. By excluding mutations that are likely to cause loss of function of the enzyme, SCANEER facilitates the identification of variants with improved enzymatic activity. Based on the results of SCANEER analysis, we can design high quality library for enzyme engineering.
Kim et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2022
3) Design and Characterization of Biosensors for the high-throughput screening
- RNA-based Biosensor & Protein-based Biosensor
: To engineer an enzyme in the metabolic pathway, the method should be able to associate the enzyme activity with the production of target metabolites, as the ultimate goal of modifying the enzyme in the biosynthetic pathway is to improve metabolite production. In addition, isolation of positive mutants from libraries is the most critical part for directed evolution of enzymes. For these reasons, genetically encoded biosensors composed of biomolecules recognizing metabolites have been proposed and developed. A biosensor is a biological device that detects specific molecules and converts the detection into a measurable signal, like fluorescence intensity or growth-coupled response. By using biosensors, high-throughput screening of metabolite producing microorganisms can be achieved. This approach provides the simple and efficient tool to engineer the pathway enzymes in metabolic engineering.
Seok JY et al., Metabolic Engineering, 2018

intro.text:
What We Work On
Our research is centered on Process Mining, Recommender Systems, and Applied AI, complemented by AI-Driven Process Innovation, Simulation & Digital Twins, and Predictive & Prescriptive Analytics.
Together, these areas enable us to understand complex processes, predict what happens next, recommend better actions, and develop intelligent solutions for real-world problems.
We develop methods to discover, analyze, predict, and improve real-world processes from event data, transforming operational data into actionable process intelligence.
Object-centric process mining and process discovery
Event abstraction, conformance checking, and predictive monitoring
Process visualization, organizational mining, and process optimization
We develop personalized and context-aware recommendation technologies that help users make better choices, with a particular focus on the fashion industry.
Personalized product, outfit, and fashion recommendation
User preference and behavioral modeling
Context-aware and AI-enhanced recommendation
We develop and apply AI and machine learning technologies to real-world problems, combining advanced models with domain knowledge and operational data.
Generative AI, large language models, and AI agents
Domain-specific foundation models
Deep learning, multimodal AI, and explainable AI
We combine process intelligence and AI to redesign how organizations operate, moving beyond process analysis toward intelligent and adaptive ways of working.
AI-assisted process redesign and improvement
Generative AI and agents for process innovation
Human–AI collaboration and intelligent workflow automation
We build data-driven simulation models and digital twins to evaluate alternatives and improve complex systems before changes are implemented in the real world.
Process digital twins and automated simulation modeling
What-if analysis and scenario evaluation
Applications in manufacturing and healthcare
We integrate prediction, optimization, and decision support to anticipate outcomes and determine what actions should be taken next.
Process performance prediction
Resource allocation and optimization
Data-driven operational decision support
Application Domains
Our research is grounded in real-world challenges and strengthened through long-term collaboration with industry and public-sector partners.
Manufacturing
We apply process mining, AI, simulation, and optimization to semiconductor manufacturing, steel production, smart factories, and other complex manufacturing systems.
Healthcare
We develop process intelligence, predictive analytics, and digital twins for clinical pathways, hospital operations, patient flows, and healthcare decision support.
Fashion
We develop AI-powered recommender systems for personalized fashion services, including product recommendation, outfit recommendation, customer preference modeling, and intelligent curation.
From Data to Impact
Our research areas are deeply interconnected. We combine process mining with AI, predictions with optimization, process data with digital twins, and recommender systems with generative AI to address complex real-world problems.
Our goal is to move from data to understanding, prediction, recommendation, innovation, and measurable real-world impact.

intro.text:
Fluid Dynamics & Numerical Analysis

We investigate a wide range of flow phenomena—flow separation and wakes around complex geometries, fluid–structure interaction (FSI), and multiphase flows—using high-fidelity numerical methods including direct numerical simulation (DNS). Our goal is to uncover the underlying physical mechanisms and to predict these phenomena with high accuracy.

HPC / GPU Computing
Media coming soon

We leverage massively parallel computing and GPU acceleration to run high-resolution flow simulations on grids of hundreds of millions of cells at high speed. By maximizing computational efficiency and scalability, we enable analyses of large-scale problems that were previously out of reach.

Turbulence & Transition Control

We control the laminar-to-turbulent transition process and near-wall flow separation through active and passive techniques. By designing and validating control strategies, we target the performance gains required in real-world applications, such as drag reduction and flow stabilization.

Design & Optimization of Aero and Power-Generation Gas Turbines
We characterize the internal flow and combustion of gas turbines used in aircraft propulsion and power generation through precise numerical analysis. Based on these results, we optimize blade geometry and operating conditions to improve efficiency and stability.

Reinforcement-Learning (AI) Control of Wind-Turbine Pitch and Yaw

We apply reinforcement-learning (AI)-based control to optimize wind-turbine blade pitch and yaw angles in real time. The goal is to maximize power output while reducing structural loads, even under fluctuating wind conditions.

Optimal Design of the Porous Transport Layer (PTL) for Hydrogen Fuel-Cell Vehicles

We optimize the microstructure of the porous transport layer (PTL), a key component of hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicles. By improving mass and heat transport, we enhance fuel-cell efficiency and durability.

Turbulence Prediction
Prediction
Ground Truth
We predict the spatiotemporal evolution of turbulent flow fields using neural-network–based models. Prediction results are compared with ground-truth simulations to verify the model’s accuracy and reliability.

Optimal Analysis & Design
We introduce machine learning to accelerate flow analysis and efficiently explore large design spaces, substantially reducing computational cost while deriving optimal designs.

Turbulence Modeling

We develop data-driven, neural-network–based turbulence models to overcome the limitations of conventional models, aiming for reliable turbulence analysis with improved predictive accuracy and generalization across diverse flow conditions.

Quantum-Native Numerical Algorithms

Time evolution of the simulated flow field (t = 1–6)

Evolution of three-dimensional vortical structures
We develop fluid-dynamics numerical algorithms optimized for the characteristics of quantum computing hardware, targeting quantum acceleration of large-scale flow problems that are intractable for classical computing.

Quantum Noise Effects
Media coming soon

We quantitatively analyze how the noise inherent in today’s quantum hardware affects the accuracy of numerical results, and study analysis techniques that remain reliable in noisy environments.

Quantum Machine Learning

Variational quantum circuit for quantum machine learning: data encoding, entangling and variational layers, and measurement-based optimization
We apply quantum machine learning to fluid-dynamics problems to explore new analysis and prediction methodologies, aiming for a next generation of computational fluid dynamics that combines quantum computing with data-driven approaches.

intro.text:
Image by Chris Morgan (JIC) Image by Heejin (POSTECH)
식물유전체재조합 연구실: 교차(crossover) 조절 연구와 식물 유전체 디자인
인류는 약 1만 년 전 식물을 재배하기 시작하며 육종(breeding)을 통해 식물을 개량해 왔다. F1 hybrid 잡종 강세와 교배 육종의 녹색혁명(Green Revolution)은 인류의 식량 안보와 보건, 그리고 평화에 기여했다. 멘델의 유전법칙, DNA의 발견에 이은 차세대 DNA 시퀀싱 기술(next-generation sequencing, NGS), 유전자 가위 기술(CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing), 기계 학습(machine learning), AI 등의 혁신적인 연구 기술 진보는 감수분열(meiosis)동안 교차 현상에 대한 이해는 물론 교차 조절, MiMe (Mitosis instead of Meiosis), hapoloid inducer, synthetic apomixis을 통해 식물 개량과 육종을 보다 가속화하고 있다. 우리는 현재 식물 유전체 디자인 시대(링크-대학신문기사)에 살고 있다.
식물 교차 패턴 연구(Mechanism of Meiotic Crossover Patterning in Plants)
식물유전체재조합 연구실은 모델 식물 애기장대와 토마토에서 교차(crossover)의 분자적 기전을 연구한다. 식물 감수분열은 꽃의 암술, 수술의 meiocyte에서 일어나며 haploid인 sperm, egg cell를 만든다. 이들 반수체 세포들은 수정을 통해 다음 세대의 diploid 식물이 된다. 특히 감수분열에서는 상동 염색체(homologous chromosome) 사이에 교차(crossing over=crossover=CO)가 일어나 자손의 유전적 다양성을 증가시키며 식물 육종에 중요한 역할을 한다. 교차는 많은 수의 DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs)에 의해서 시작하지만 이들 DSBs 중 약 5% 정도만이 DBS 수선 과정을 거쳐 교차가 된다. 따라서, 상동 염색체상의 교차 수는 염색체 분리를 위해 1개는 필수적이지만 그 이상은 억제되어 1개 또는 2개가 주로 일어나며 3개인 경우도 드물다 (동.식물, ~1.5-2.0 COs per chromosome pair). 또한 상동 염색체 사이에 드물게 두 개의 교차가 발생하더라도 두 개의 교차는 교차 간섭(crossover interference) 현상으로 인해 서로 멀리 떨어져서 발생한다. 즉 두 개의 교차가 가깝게 일어나는 일은 거의 없다. 또한 교차는 pericentromere에서 더욱 드물게 일어난다. 이러한 교차 수와 빈도, 교차 패턴은 교차 촉진자(pro-crossover factors), 교차 억제자(anti-crossover factors) 및 epigenetic factor들(H3K9me2/non-CG methylation, H2A.W: PNAS)에 의해 조절된다. 따라서 식물 교차의 패턴 연구를 통한 교차 수와 위치 조절은 apomixis, haploid inducer, reverse breeding과 함께 새로운 육종 기술 개발에 매우 중요한 기여를 한다. 특히, 교차 간섭 현상은 20세기 초에 발견됐지만 분자적 기전은 오랫동안 미궁이었다. 하지만 최근에 synaptonemal complex의 components와 pro-crossover E3 ligase HEI10이 교차 간섭을 매개하고 있음이 밝혀졌다. 우리 연구실은 교차 수와 교차 간섭을 조절하는 새로운 교차 조절 인자(HCR1, HCR2, HCR3, HCR7)를 유전학적으로 발굴하고 최첨단 유전체학, 세포학, 분자생물학적 연구 기법들을 통해 교차 패턴의 기초 연구를 수행중이며, 이를 토마토의 교차 조절에도 적용하고 있다.
최첨단 교차 재조합 연구 방법
새로운 교차율 증가 돌연변이 발굴 및 연구: 교차 재조합의 분자적 기전을 밝히기 위해서 우리는 교차 빈도 증가(high crossover rate, hcr) 또는 감소하는 돌연변이들을 찾는 유전학적 스크리닝을 수행해오고 있다. 특히 형광 종자 및 형광 꽃가루 교차 리포터 시스템(seed or pollen fluorescence tagged lines, FTLs)을 활용하고 딥러닝 기반 이미지 분석을 통해 교차 빈도를 정교하고 신속하고 대량으로 분석이 가능하다. 돌연변이원으로는 EMS, activation-tagging 을 활용한다 (hcr3:Nature Plants, hcr2:EMBO J, hcr1:Nature Plants)
고해상도 유전체 수준의 교차 지도 작성 (High-resolution Genome-wide Crossover Mapping): short-read와 long-read next-generation sequencing 기술을 활용하여 96개 F2 식물체들을 동시에 시퀀싱하여 교차 위치를 정확히 탐지한다 (genotyping-by-sequencing, GBS; Nanopore seq를 이용한 COmapper: New Phytologist).
Immuno-cytology: 교차 과정은 감수분열 동안 염색체의 움직임과 구조 변화와 연관되어 있다. DSB 형성 시 leptotene은 axis-loop 구조를 만들고, 이후 DSB 수선 시 zygotene의 상동염색체는 pairing이 일어나고 pachytene에서는 상동염색체간 synaptonemal complex를 통해 synapsis를 이룬다. 교차는 pachytene 말기와 diplotene, diakinesis에서 MLH1의 immunostaining을 통해 확인이 가능하다. 또한 axis element, DSB foci, ZMMs (pro-crossover factors)들 역시 immunocytology을 통해 확인한다.
Genomic approaches: SPO11-oligo sequencing, pollen-typing, mei-ChIP seq, Nuc-seq, ATAC seq, mei-INTACT, meiMIGS, meiOE, mei-dCas9-Suntag/VP64 or SRDX, COmapper 등 새로운 연구 기법들을 활용하고 개발한다.
Meiosis is fundamental to sexual reproduction and produces genetic diversity in progeny. Meiotic recombination is initiated by programmed DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) formation. The repair of DSBs leads to crossovers or non-crossovers via DSB repair. Despite the induction of excess DSBs, only a subset matures to crossovers. Anti-recombination factors restrict crossovers while interference causes even-spaced crossover patterns by preventing the coincidence of crossovers in the same chromosomes. The DSBs and crossovers are non-uniform along chromosomes, typically occurring at narrow regions, called recombination hotspots. Plant meiotic recombination hotspots occur at gene promoters and terminators in euchromatin while heterochromatin is suppressed, indicating that chromatin structure influences recombination distribution (Choi et. al., 2013 Nature genetics, Choi et. al., 2018 Genome Research). Notably, the meiotic recombination process requires dynamic assembly and disassembly of meiotic protein complexes in time and space.
We aim to understand mechanistically how meiotic recombination is controlled by the interplay between meiotic proteins and the higher order of chromosome structure. To achieve this, we apply advanced methods of recombination measurements at different scales from single base-pair to genome (SPO11-oligonucleotide seq (~bp), pollen typing (~10 kb), fluorescent seed and pollen reporter systems (~1-5 Mb), genotyping-by-sequencing (genome)). We have performed a forward genetic screen of high crossover rate mutants (hcr1, hcr2, hcr3, hcr6 and hcr7) using high-throughput fluorescent seed-scoring and tetrad analysis in Arabidopsis and chracterized them (hcr3:Nature Plants, hcr2:EMBO J, hcr1:Nature Plants). We have also developed "DeepTetrad", a deep learning-based image recognition package for pollen tetrad analysis that enables high-throughput measurements of crossover frequency and interference in individual plants. In addition, we are intensively using the CRISPR/Cas9 system, which allows us to edit the genome and control gene expression for studying meiotic recombination in plants.
Our studies on meiotic recombination can help accelerate plant breeding for crop improvement by recombining or mapping useful genetic variations that occur spontaneously or as a result of mutagenesis in wild-type plant accessions at particular areas and diverse domesticated varieties. New combinations of DNA variations contributing to crop productivity, disease resistance, fruit, and grain quality can be generated by increasing crossover frequency between tightly linked alleles that had been hardly recombined along a chromosome. Once useful DNA variations are identified by genetic mapping by increasing crossovers, a CRISPR/Cas9 system can also be applied to edit plant genomes of elite varieties.

intro.text:
About Prof. Kim, Tae-Hwan
Prof. Tae-Hwan Kim is a Full Professor at the Department of Physics at Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH) in Pohang, South Korea. He received his Ph.D. in physics from Seoul National University in 2005, where he studied spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy under the supervision of Prof. Young Kuk. From 2006 to 2010, he worked at the Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences (CNMS) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, investigating nanoscale transport properties of various nanostructures at low temperatures using low-temperature four-probe scanning tunneling microscopy under the guidance of Dr. An-Ping Li. He then served as a Collegiate Assistant Professor at POSTECH from 2010 to 2013, focusing on one-dimensional atomic wires in collaboration with Prof. Han Woong Yeom. Since joining the POSTECH faculty in 2013, Prof. Kim has concentrated his research on topological edge states in low-dimensional electronic systems. Notably, he and his colleagues discovered chiral solitons in indium atomic wires, characterizing their structural and electronic properties, and proposed topological operations using chiral solitons for next-generation information devices. His research interests also encompass two-dimensional materials such as graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides. Prof. Kim has co-authored publications in esteemed peer-reviewed journals, including Science, Nature Physics, and Physical Review Letters.

intro.text:
Encoded Library Technology
- 암호화 라이브러리 기술(encoded library technology)은 표적 단백질에 결합하는 리간드를 매우 빠르고 효율적으로 발굴함으로써, 신약후보물질을 빠르게 확보할 수 있게 해주는 핵심적인 신약개발 기술입니다.
- 대표적인 암호화 라이브러리 기술로서, DNA-암호화 라이브러리 기술(DNA-encoded library)이 있습니다. 이 기술에서는 라이브러리 화합물과, 각 화합물에 대한 구조적인 정보를 암호화(encoding)하고 있는 암호화 물질(DNA)이 연결되어 있는 형태로 라이브러리 분자가 존재합니다. 즉, 암호화 물질은 바코드(barcode)와 같은 역할을 하여, 이 바코드가 의미하는 화합물이 어떤 구조인지를 알 수 있게 해줍니다. 스크리닝 이후, 암호화 물질의 서열을 차세대 염기서열 분석법(next-generation sequencing)을 통해 분석하여, 해당 암호화 물질이 암호화하고 있는 화합물의 구조(스크리닝 이후 단백질에 결합한 화합물)을 밝혀낼 수 있습니다.
- 기존 신약개발에 많이 사용되어 온 고효율 스크리닝(high-throughput screening) 방법과 달리, 이와 같은 암호화 라이브러리 기술을 활용하면, 수십억 개 이상의 다양한 구조의 화합물을 빠르게 선별함으로써 단기간에 최적의 신약후보물질을 매우 빠르게 도출할 수 있습니다.
본 연구실은 독자저인 유전자 암호화 라이브러리의 합성, 초고효율 스크리닝 기술 및 데이터 분석을 통한 신약후보물질 발굴 등, 암호화 라이브러리 기술을 종합적으로 보유하고 있습니다. 본 연구실은 이러한 암호화 라이브러리 기술을 주제로 대형 정부과제를 진행하고 있으며, 정부출연연구소(한국화학연구원 및 한국생명공학연구원), 대학, 제약회사 등과의 협업을 진행하고 있습니다.
- 이와 같은 기술력을 바탕으로, 궁극적으로 차세대 신약개발 기반 기술을 확보하는 것을 목표로 하고 있습니다.

Targeted Protein Degradation (TPD)
- 표적 단백질 분해 (TPD) 기술은 세포 내에서 불필요한 단백질의 분해를 담당하는 ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS)을 활용하여 질병을 유발하는 표적 단백질을 분해함으로써, 질병을 치료하는 새로운 개념의 신약개발 기술입니다.
- 대표적인 TPD 기술로서 PROTAC (Proteolysis-Targeting Chimera)이 있습니다. PROTAC은 표적단백질에 결합하는 small-molecule과 E3 ligase에 결합하는 ligand가 연결된 bifunctional한 구조를 가지고 있습니다. 따라서, 이 물질은 표적단백질과 E3 ligase에 동시에 결합함으로써 두 단백질 간의 close proximity를 유발하여, 최종적으로 표적단백질의 ubiquitination 및 proteasomal degradation을 유도하게 됩니다.
- 이러한 TPD는 기존 약물과 달리 catalytic하게 질병-유발 단백질을 분해함으로써, 낮은 약물 농도에서도 매우 효과적으로 치료 효과를 나타낼 수 있습니다.
- 본 연구실은 최근 ‘표적단백질 분해 융합물질 개발’ 이라는 주제로 대형 정부과제를 수주하였으며, 연세대학교 및 고려대학교 연구팀과 함께 신개념 TPD 플랫폼 개발을 선도하고 있습니다.
- 더 나아가, 이러한 혁신적인 신약개발 플랫폼을 통해 암이나 비만 등 다양한 난치성 질환에 대한 치료제를 개발하고 있습니다.

intro.text:
Nano Emerging Materials and Hybrid Devices Lab.
CJ Kim Group
Our Mission
Nanoscale materials, whose functionalities arise from their unique atomic configurations and small sizes, lie at the heart of addressing a wide range of engineering challenges. Our mission is to develop versatile and scalable techniques to artificially design materials with atomic-level precision—surpassing the capabilities of current state-of-the-art methods. We investigate novel properties in these materials and explore their potential applications in emerging technologies.

우리 연구실은 그래핀과 2차원 반도체처럼 원자층 두께의 얇은 소재를 중심으로, 다양한 나노 소재의 구조를 원자 수준에서 정밀하게 제어하고 효율적으로 합성하는 방법을 연구합니다. 이를 통해 새로운 물질과 물성을 탐색하고, 차세대 반도체 소자와 양자 소자 구현에 도전합니다. 새로운 소재를 직접 만들고, 그 안의 흥미로운 현상을 발견하며, 미래 기술로 연결하는 연구를 함께하며 성장할 대학원생 및 연구원들을 모집합니다.
현재 박사 후 연구원 (전공: 화공, 물리, 화학, 재료) 상시 모집 중이며, 2027년 봄 학기 입학을 위한 대학원생 통합 과정 (이공계, 전공 무관) 2명을 모집 중입니다. (2명 초과시에는 개별 상담결과에 따라 추가 입학 가능) 이 밖에도 학사 연구 참여생도 모집 중이니 관심있는 학생들은 위 연락처로 연락바랍니다.

We are an interdisciplinary research group in the Department of Chemical Engineering at POSTECH. We develop innovative platforms for designing nanomaterials at the atomic scale through growth, assembly, and chemical processing. We study the fundamental properties of artificial materials with the aid of state-of-the-art characterization tools and fabricate emerging nanodevices with advanced functionalities.
Growths of 2D Materials
We grow 2D materials with nanoscale uniformity over large areas using chemical vapor deposition processes to provide key elements for nanotechnology. In addition to the epitaxial growth of highly crystalline materials, we aim to grow materials with designed disorders and thermodynamically metastable phases by developing new growth techniques.
Atomic-scale Structural Engineering
Arbitrary control of material structures with atomic-scale precision lies at the heart of nanoelectronics and photonics, encompassing interface engineering for devices, the development of metamaterials, and the artificial construction of new materials. We aim to develop new toolsets with additional structural degrees of freedom to enable designs beyond the capabilities of current techniques.

Discovery of
Nano-material Properties
Emerging nanomaterials can offer novel and enhanced physical and chemical properties that bulk materials do not. We explore these properties by studying materials fabricated in our lab. Our goals involve discoveries of new high-mobility semiconductors, ultrathin glass with exceptional mechanical toughness, and chemically active electronic and optical materials with high sensitivity and selectivity.
Emerging Nano Devices
Emerging Nano Devices
While emerging nanomaterials can be integrated with existing device platforms to enable novel architectures, techniques customized for the target materials must be developed to achieve optimum device performance. We develop such techniques for specific nanomaterials and realize non-conventional nanodevices, such as atomically thin field-effect transistors, electronic molecular sensors, and devices based on ion transport.

Rechargeable battery systems
Efficient generation and transportation of energy is now the most important task of our time. Rechargeable battery systems using lithium-, sodium- or potassium-ions have received a great deal of attention in industry as well as academia due to their high energy density and reliability, but there are still some issues to be solved. In our laboratory, we are investigating the operating principle of batteries and researching to design more efficient energy storage systems.

Material Science & Energy Storage
The "active material" of the electrode primarily determines the energy density, power density, cycle life, and safety of the battery. So we can say that understanding the basics of active materials is of the utmost importance! Here we design and find next-generation materials to create a clean future.

Electrochemistry of Materials
The electrochemical reaction from the material is too complicated. We need to not only understand the charge transfer at the surface but also consider the ion diffusion in the solid. In addition, since the battery system is made up of many-body particle electrodes, unforeseen phenomena may be discovered. We understand the basics of electrochemical reactions.

intro.text:
Immune receptors
대표적인 immune receptor인 Toll-like receptor(TLR)는 박테리아나 바이러스에서 유래되는 lipoprotein/lipopolysaccharide/flagellin/nucleic acids 등을 인식하여, 초기 감염을 감지하고 면역시스템을 활성화시키는 역할을 합니다. TLR이 활성화되면 MyD88와 TRIF 신호전달 과정을 통해 면역세포가 활성화되고 cytokine, chemokine, type-1 IFN 등을 분비하여 강력한 선천성 면역반응을 일으킵니다. TLR은 선천성면역 연구와 항체신약개발에 중요하지만, 어떠한 구조변화를 통하여 활성화 되는지에 대한 메커니즘은 여전히 불확실합니다. 이처럼 많은 경우 중요하게 여겨지지만 메커니즘이 규명되지 않은 면역 수용체들이 많습니다. 저희 연구실에서는 다양한 리간드에 의한 신호전달 복합체 assembly 및 clustering을 연구하고 있으며, 이러한 연구를 통해 면역 수용체들의 신호전달 메커니즘을 밝히고, 패혈증, 바이러스 감염, 암 발생을 억제할 수 있는 항체 신약을 개발하고자 합니다.

Antibody engineering
항체는 구조생물학과 신약개발에 중요한 역할을 합니다. 가속기를 이용한 단백질 구조연구를 위해서는 결정상태의 샘플이 필요한데, 결정화가 어려운 표적단백질이 많습니다. 이러한 표적에 항체를 결합시켜주면 결정화를 유도할 수 있습니다. 최근 10년간 전자현미경 기술의 발전으로 단백질 구조연구에 극저온 전자현미경 (cryo-EM)을 사용할 수 있게 되었고 이 때문에 구조생물학에 새로운 시대가 열렸습니다. 항체는 cryo-EM 연구에서도 중요한 역할을 합니다. cryo-EM 연구를 위해서는 표적단백질의 크기가 ~50 kDa 이상 되어야 합니다. 이보다 작은 표적단백질의 경우에 항체를 결합시켜 주면 전체 크기가 증가하기 때문에 cryo-EM 구조연구에 사용할 수 있습니다. 항체는 단백질 구조연구뿐만 아니라 신약개발의 목표이기도 합니다. 작년 세계 10대 의약품의 절반이 항체를 이용한 항체신약 입니다. 항체와 표적 단백질의 결합 구조를 규명하면 분자 모델링을 이용하여 항체의 성능을 향상시킬 수 있습니다. 저희 연구실은 항체를 단백질 구조연구와 신약개발에 적합하도록 변형시키는 연구를 수행하고 있습니다.
